item.title: The end of humanity
item.dc:creator: Psyche Video
item.description:
Instead of accepting that humanity will soon be obsolete, we can build a better future with respect for human traditions

- A film by Andreas Dürr and Jan-Marc Furer

Watch on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
A choir of tech titans and influential commentators has grown inescapably loud with proclamations that technology will soon render humanity, in its current form, obsolete. This leaves each of us with a binary choice: embrace the coming ‘post-human paradigm’ or get left behind. Created by the Swiss filmmakers Andreas Dürr and Jan-Marc Furer, The End of Humanity pushes back against the idea that we can, or should, be so easily replaced. Integrating cinematic sci-fi flourishes and interviews with philosophers, theologians and other leading thinkers, the documentary argues that corporate incentives, a compliant press and a fundamental misunderstanding of humanity itself have pushed conversations about the future towards fatalism. Instead, the film makes the case that the future is far from settled: we needn’t eschew technology entirely, but should build it in a way that respects our intellectual traditions, preserves our humanity and, in so doing, engenders a better future.

This short is condensed from a feature-length version of The End of Humanity.

item.title: When you feel moral disgust, what’s the emotion telling you?
item.dc:creator: Brandon Yip
item.description:
Some actions and words provoke instant revulsion. To know if we can trust that gut feeling, we should probe why we have it

- by Brandon Yip

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
‘Disgusting’ and similar words are flung across political divides quite often today. For example, the US president Donald Trump has used the word to describe his political opponents, journalists and others. And many have voiced disgust at the president’s own behaviours. For instance, after viewing Trump’s altercation with the Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy during a press conference in 2025, the author David Brooks described feeling ‘nauseated, just nauseated’. In politics and beyond, expressing disgust is a common response to actions that one finds deeply objectionable, such as racist rhetoric, acts of sexual abuse or policies that harm vulnerable people.

Rather than see expressions like these as merely rhetorical, many philosophers and psychologists argue that moral disgust is a distinct and significant kind of moral response. The distinction between moral disgust and regular disgust lies in the way their objects are experienced by the disgusted person. People feel regular disgust in response to the spread of filth, which motivates physical avoidance and cleansing. The stench of urine on a train, for example, provokes this kind of disgust. When people feel moral disgust, it’s as if they are experiencing a sort of moral pollution, which motivates them to socially avoid and exclude the target of the disgust. Betrayal and exploitation, for example, often provoke moral disgust, but not regular disgust.

Many scholars believe that disgust operates based on simplistic and unreliable heuristics. For example, in his book Yuck!: The Nature and Moral Significance of Disgust (2011), the philosopher Daniel Kelly argues that disgust is an evolutionarily old mechanism that protected humans from poisons and parasites – and so it operates on a ‘hair trigger’ that is prone to generate false positives. Kelly thinks that, since moral disgust grew out of regular disgust, it is similarly unreliable when it comes to moral matters. Just as you can find some physical thing disgusting (say, a certain kind of cheese) when it’s actually harmless, you might automatically find some behaviours morally disgusting that, on reflection, aren’t so bad.

Now, some of Kelly’s premises can be challenged: there is evidence that our emotional systems are intelligent and adaptable. Rather than just recapitulating ancient functions, our emotions contain updating mechanisms that enable them to respond to new physical and social challenges. Furthermore, even regular disgust is flexible and remarkably sensitive to context. For example, whether you find saliva disgusting depends a lot on whether it comes from your lover or a total stranger.

Some have argued that, far from being unreliable, moral disgust plays an invaluable role in moral judgment. In Leon Kass’s classic essay ‘The Wisdom of Repugnance’ (1997), he claims that people’s disgust towards human cloning gives us some reason to avoid that practice, warning us ‘not to transgress what is unspeakably profound’. In this decadent age, Kass says, ‘repugnance may be the only voice left that speaks up to defend the central core of our humanity.’

So, is feeling morally disgusted by an act or a practice something that we should take seriously as a sign that it is morally problematic? To answer this, we need to first get clear on why people feel moral disgust – what exactly it alerts us to.

Contemporary philosophers have offered various explanations of what moral disgust does, though each of these has limitations. In Alexandra Plakias’s account, for example, moral disgust is a response to behaviours that are socially contagious: norm-violating behaviours, such as acts of physical violence, that might spread through a population if left unchecked. This is a compelling idea, but upon further examination, the relationship between socially contagious behaviours and moral disgust appears to be tenuous. Many norm violations that could be socially contagious – such as stealing office supplies or not declaring tips as taxable income – don’t tend to strike people as morally disgusting.

Presenting a different view of moral disgust, Victor Kumar suggests that it’s a response to behaviours that undermine relations of trust and reciprocity. He is certainly right that behaviours that undermine cooperative relations, such as betraying one’s compatriots or unfairly dividing rewards, are often seen as morally disgusting. Yet there are also many other acts that people find morally disgusting – such as cannibalism, or incest among consenting adults – that do not involve a failure of reciprocity.

Imagine you’re in a soccer game with players who are randomly picking up the ball and throwing it around

I believe that John Kekes was on the right path with a suggestion he put forth in the 1990s. Kekes proposed that moral disgust enforces moral taboos – prohibitions against the kinds of actions that endanger the very possibility of civilised life. These violations supposedly ‘threaten to bring about a form of life in which moral considerations have no foothold.’ This seems somewhat overblown: after all, civilisations have repeatedly survived the violation of moral taboos. But perhaps what moral disgust does is guard against the collapse of particular forms of rule-structured life.

To see what I mean, consider the relationship between our personal behaviours and the social worlds that we inhabit. A social world is structured by rules and norms that people have internalised and adopted. Tamar Schapiro points out that these normative orders are sustained by individuals’ compliance with the rules. A judge who continues to follow legal procedure – even when they could choose to act corruptly – helps to sustain the larger normative structure that gives the judge’s actions legitimacy.

If norm compliance keeps important social structures intact, then perhaps certain actions can undermine them. Imagine that you are trying to play soccer with players who are randomly picking up the ball and throwing it around. Such behaviour not only violates the rules of the game, it undermines the game itself. Something analogous happens in typical cases of moral disgust, where the stakes are higher. In explaining his nausea at seeing Trump behave ‘vilely’ toward Zelenskyy and US allies, for example, Brooks suggested that Trump was unravelling a benign, US-centred international order and replacing it with one where ‘might makes right’. Let’s call actions that undermine a social order socially corrosive.

My proposal, then, is this: moral disgust is a response to behaviour that is socially corrosive. More precisely, when some behaviour undermines a set of moral norms that a person is attuned to, they feel morally disgusted.

The moral norms you are attuned to are those that appear to you to impose genuine constraints on behaviour. Your attunement to these norms might be strong and overt – you might explicitly endorse your culture’s norms against using corporal punishment on children, for example. Or, your attunement might be merely implicit. If you grew up in an Islamic culture that sees eating pork as morally disgusting, but then you left Islam, you might still continue to experience the pork prohibition as having some force. People can also become attuned to new norms. An adult Muslim convert – or a vegan – could come to acquire moral disgust towards pork-eating.

Behaviours once seen as morally disgusting, such as premarital sex, are now widely seen as acceptable

When I suggest that morally disgusting actions undermine some social order, I mean that they threaten to stop a community from operating with some set of moral norms. For example, if a political leader engages in corruption or an employer openly flirts with his employees, then the norms that govern that society or that workplace will be undermined as long as such behaviour goes unchecked. This possibility is more serious than just contagious norm-violation; it is not simply that more corruption or more creepy flirting is forthcoming. It’s that the rule of law or respectful workplace interactions become tenuous altogether. Moral disgust alerts us to the fact that certain behaviours might corrode the moral norms that we care about, and it motivates us to sanction or exclude those who behave in those ways.

With this in mind, it is worth returning to Kass’s article about cloning and disgust. He notes that human beings have ‘systems of identity and relationship on the bases of … deep natural facts of begetting,’ and suggests that cloning would confound ‘all normal understandings of father, mother, sibling, grandparent, etc.’ To Kass, then, what is problematic is not just the wrongness of cloning in itself or its mere proliferation. Rather, accepting cloning would unravel a set of norms governing human relations.

Could cloning really undermine all that? It’s not as implausible as it might seem. Already, the norms surrounding sex and the family have undergone radical transformation over the past century. Behaviours once seen by many as morally disgusting, such as premarital sex or homosexuality, are now widely seen as morally acceptable. This has produced profound changes in the meaning of marriage and sex. Even if we consider these changes liberating – welcome alterations to an overly constricting social order – these examples show how it’s plausible that a broader set of moral norms (such as those structuring families) is susceptible to change once key norms (such as those governing procreation or sex) become undone.

Clearly, we should not uncritically endorse the deliverances of moral disgust. One may, for example, decide that the familial structure that Kass protects is an unjust and patriarchal one. The norms we are attuned to are a mixed bag that includes both aspirational ideals that bend towards justice, as well as the nastier parts of our cultures.

Yet it is still worth listening to our moral guts – carefully. Moral disgust sometimes provides a signal that something is deeply wrong, even when one’s capacity for moral reasoning has been compromised. Ditte Marie Munch-Jurisic has noted, for example, that the perpetrators of heinous crimes often react with disgust toward their own actions. Under the Nazi regime, some soldiers and citizens experienced sheer revulsion in carrying out their role in the Holocaust. They suppressed this revulsion with reasons provided by the ideological narratives of the Nazi regime. Similarly, Miranda Fricker has shown that injustice sometimes makes it hard to understand the conditions of oppression. For example, prior to acquiring the concept of sexual harassment, many women struggled to articulate the problematic nature of men’s inappropriate advances. But they were morally disgusted by such behaviour, even before they could fully explain why it was wrong – including how it undermined norms of equal respect for men and women.

If there is a wisdom in moral disgust, then, it is an ambivalent one that we should not always heed, yet cannot simply ignore. Unfortunately, there isn’t a simple formula to tell us whether moral disgust is highlighting something important or leading us astray. When we feel or encounter moral revulsion, we should neither dismiss it as mere primitive reaction nor treat the emotion as having an infallible moral authority. Instead, we ought to pause and reflect on what we are actually responding to. We should try to articulate the normative order that our revulsion is guarding – and then ask ourselves whether or not we have good reasons to cherish it.

item.title: Can he teach the teachers?
item.dc:creator: Nancy Averett
item.description:
The neuroscientist Stanislas Dehaene wants to bring four decades of findings on how the brain learns into the classroom. But evidence alone can’t overcome the politics in education

- by Nancy Averett

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
Stanislas Dehaene enters a small library inside the mansion that houses the French ministry of education. Autumn light filters down from a skylight, illuminating glass-fronted bookshelves holding the journaux officiels – the laws, decrees, regulations and rules of the French Republic. Dehaene takes his place and flips open his laptop as members file in.

As president of the Scientific Council for National Education, a body charged with advising the government on evidence-based learning, Dehaene has a pressing concern: Le Monde has just accused the Council of racism. As he shares this news, the warmth in his voice disappears, replaced by something sharper.

He asks the group to share his rebuttal on social media because Le Monde has declined to print it. ‘I find it ridiculous that we have to waste time responding to such things,’ he says. ‘It’s an accusation completely beside the truth.’

A world-renowned cognitive neuroscientist, Dehaene has published hundreds of refereed journal articles and seven books for general readers on reading, mathematics, consciousness and learning. More than a decade ago, he set out to do something that sounded straightforward: take four decades of research mapping how the brain learns, and compel education systems to follow its insights. He thought the evidence would speak for itself. Instead, he has run into the deeply human resistance of politics, identity and belief. In France, more than one in four children arrive at secondary school without a firm grasp of reading or mathematics. Dehaene does not see these as abstract statistics but rather as the cost children pay for that resistance.

‘It’s been eight years, and the scores of French children are changing a tiny little bit,’ he says with a deep sigh. ‘It’s very, very difficult. The social forces are enormous.’

The previous day, I visited him at his brain-imaging lab, NeuroSpin, in the Parisian suburb of Saclay, where he took me down a hallway known as ‘magnet street’ to the facility’s massive MRI equipment. He paused outside the control room of the newest MRI magnet, an 11.7-tesla scanner, one of the strongest human-rated machines in the world, which displays the brain in finer anatomical detail than ever seen before. A loud mechanical buzz pulsed in the hallway – the vibration of the magnet’s electromagnetic coils. ‘Do you have a pacemaker or anything like that?’ he asked before opening the door.

Inside, researchers huddled around computer screens, and a video monitor displayed a fuzzy image of the tube’s interior. It’s one thing to get adults to lie down in the noisy, claustrophobic setting of an MRI tube, but Dehaene, along with his wife, the paediatrician Ghislaine Dehaene-Lambertz, has worked hard to make children comfortable in this setting.

That instinct to observe a child closely would shape Dehaene’s future work

In one experiment, they put three-month-olds in the tube – the babies had just been fed, wore headphones, and were placed in a specially designed cradle – and played them short sentences, some spoken normally and some played backward, a way to strip out language’s meaning while keeping its raw sound intact. The results, published in Science in 2002, showed that the brain’s architecture for language – the same left-hemisphere regions active in adult brains – was already in place and functioning at three months. ‘Before our work, people barely knew if the cortex was working or not,’ Dehaene says.

He met Ghislaine Lambertz in 1986 while both were working in the lab of Jacques Mehler, a pioneer in cognitive psychology. They became part of a group that met at Mehler’s apartment for dinners of pasta and good wine, and they married within a year – Dehaene laughs while sharing that, a few months after the ceremony, their first son, Guillaume, was born. Dehaene was just 21 and, while he had landed his first job, he still hadn’t defended his dissertation. ‘My son was at my PhD defence,’ he says. ‘So I guess the order is kid, permanent position, PhD.’

After Guillaume, two more sons, David and Olivier, followed. When Olivier was five, his preschool teacher taught him to write his first name, and he proudly signed all of his artwork. Half the time, though, he wrote the letters right to left. The scientist in Dehaene was fascinated; the father was anxious. Was this a sign of incipient dyslexia? Olivier’s backward writing soon disappeared on its own. But that instinct to observe a child closely, to take seriously any unusual turns in their learning behaviour that might signal a problem, would shape Dehaene’s future work.

So would Ghislaine. Over the years, she and Dehaene have built a body of research tracing the brain’s relationship with language from infancy through the first years of reading. Dehaene showed me his wife’s lab, opening a closet where she kept tiny caps fitted with electrodes that could be slipped over a baby’s head to read brainwaves. ‘We divided the field between us,’ he said. ‘You know, she is going to do babies, and I won’t touch it, and I will do adults … but of course we mixed in all sorts of ways until we joined in the middle.’

After the tour, we headed to his office, which holds several 3D-printed models of his brain – including one that lay in a pool of powdery plaster dust, the lasagna-like folds of the cortex fractured. Dehaene told me that a photojournalist had asked him to pose with it, and he stumbled and dropped it. ‘The guy started taking pictures like crazy,’ he says. ‘Well, that was the end of my brain.’

Dehaene often punctuates his thoughts with a high-pitched laugh, eyes sparkling, dimples flashing. The effect is disarming. He turned 61 this May but looks years younger – a lean, agile man with a bald pate and delicate wire-rimmed glasses who sometimes wears a tiny red rosette on his lapel signifying his membership in the French Legion of Honour.

Former students and colleagues call Dehaene a genius. At a recent conference, Andreas Nieder, a German neurobiologist, told the audience: ‘Whenever I talk with him, I have the impression that his brain is ticking along at twice the frequency of mine.’ Later, Ghislaine joked that Dehaene’s productivity suggests that he must have cloned himself. ‘In fact, there are two Stans!’

‘I believe in the expansion of the human mind. I believe this is an extraordinary machine. We should realise its full potential’

Dehaene dismisses such praise. When I ask whether he was simply born with a better brain, his voice softens, and he turns serious – echoing the point he was trying to make in his rebuttal to Le Monde – ‘No, I don’t think so,’ he says. ‘We scan different people, and we see the same circuits … for reading or for mathematics … I’m sure if we dig deeper, we’d find individual differences, but there is a universal organisation. I don’t think I’m different at all in that respect.’

As he has uncovered more and more of the brain’s secrets, Dehaene has developed a deep sense of awe over its capabilities. At the same time, he has become aware of how important it is to nurture those neurons when they are malleable. In his book Seeing the Mind (2023), he describes his delight in watching his four granddaughters develop, knowing that ‘their dendritic trees grow by several billion synapses every day … Their tiny brains are unmatched learning machines.’

That reverence is not without anguish: if a society fails to engage a brain this extraordinary, during the precise window when it matters most – childhood – then it’s condemning a portion of its population to a diminished intellectual life. ‘I believe in the expansion of the human mind,’ Dehaene says, tapping his desk in agitation. ‘I believe this is an extraordinary machine. We should realise its full potential – otherwise it’s a terrible waste.’

Dehaene grew up in Roubaix, a struggling industrial city in northern France, where his father, Philippe Dehaene, a paediatrician, was determined to make up for any deficiencies in the local schools. The elder Dehaene brought home books and magazines akin to Scientific American and National Geographic. He stretched the family budget to buy his sons one of the earliest personal computers, a Tandy TRS-80. ‘It changed my life,’ Dehaene says. ‘I became very active and independent in programming my own stuff, my own games, my own math.’

As a teenager, Dehaene was hired by local families to tutor their children in mathematics. Fractions came easily to him, but the children he helped found them impenetrable. He still wonders what makes some mathematical operations so difficult. ‘We’re still working on it in the lab right now,’ he adds.

His father shaped more than his curiosity. By the mid-1960s, researchers had linked alcohol consumption during pregnancy to physical and cognitive disabilities in infants – something many clinicians dismissed as harmless. By the early 1970s, Philippe Dehaene was studying fetal alcohol syndrome – the world’s leading preventable cause of intellectual disability – and warning the public about it. It was a lesson that would stay with his son: that patiently gathering evidence and stubbornly arguing for it might protect children whom institutions had failed to notice.

After high school, Dehaene won a spot at the elite École normale supérieure in Paris. A few years later, after earning degrees in mathematics and computer science, he realised that, although he loved math, he was particularly interested in figuring out how the brain does math. So he joined Mehler’s lab as a doctoral student, becoming the only cognitive psychology researcher there studying numbers and the brain.

Dehaene found it thrilling to work with two brilliant but opposing thinkers

Susana Franck, who co-edited the journal Cognition with Mehler, recalls messy desks piled with papers and an earnest young man – Dehaene was measuring college students’ reaction times as they chose the higher or lower of two numbers. ‘I have many recollections of being kidnapped into listening to numbers on the loudspeaker of the black computer, and having to say which was the larger or smaller,’ Franck says with a laugh. She and the other subjects easily distinguished numbers far apart, like 1 and 9, but struggled with closer pairs, such as 5 and 6. Even mathematics majors faltered, suggesting the difficulty reflected a structural property of the brain, rather than education.

Dehaene also attended lectures at the Collège de France, the country’s most prestigious research institution. He was particularly drawn to presentations by the neuroscientist Jean-Pierre Changeux, whose bestseller, Neuronal Man (1983), advanced the radical idea that the mind is nothing more than its biology. One day in the lecture hall, someone handed Dehaene a piece of paper on which Changeux had scribbled: ‘Please meet me after class.’ The eminent scientist was looking for a mathematician to create a computer model of how the brain represents numbers. ‘I said yes immediately,’ Dehaene says.

One of the model’s predictions was the existence of neurons that respond to specific numbers, firing robustly for their preferred quantity and less so for numbers further away. This gradient helped explain why Dehaene’s subjects were struggling to distinguish close numbers – a neuron tuned to 5 would also fire somewhat strongly for 4 and 6, less so for 1 or 9. (Fifteen years later, Nieder tested the theory in monkeys and found exactly what the model predicted.)

Dehaene found it thrilling to work with two brilliant but opposing thinkers. Mehler favoured studying behaviour to infer how the brain produces thought; Changeux argued for mapping neurons directly. ‘They disagreed about everything,’ Dehaene says. ‘And I was in the middle.’ He decided he must somehow combine both.

The resolution came in 1988 as he was flipping through Nature and came upon a study by American researchers who had used PET scans to track changes in cerebral blood flow while patients listened to or read single words. He snapped to attention: the article described how scientists had watched a proxy for thought flicker across a living brain.

‘You know how people have flashbulb memories?’ he says. ‘I have one of reading that paper – I can almost see the journal and where I was sitting.’

Dehaene soon decamped to the University of Oregon for a postdoc with Michael Posner, one of the Nature paper’s authors. Dehaene spent two years there learning to combine brain scanning – which in those days required injecting the patient with a radioactive tracer – with behavioural experiments.

In 1994, he moved back to Paris, eager to return to number research. There, he continued his collaboration with Laurent Cohen, a colleague from Mehler’s lab, who had access to patients with brain lesions that affected their number perception. Some could read the symbol ‘7’ but had no sense of its quantity. Others could estimate ‘about 7’ when shown a cluster of dots, but couldn’t recall the answer to a problem like 7 × 8 = 56. The two researchers concluded that the brain contains three separate but interconnected number systems: one for visual symbols, one for words, and one for approximate quantities.

Children counting on fingers is in fact a scaffold to the abstract, not a crutch

One of those patients, whom Dehaene later described as ‘Mr N’, had a lesion in the back of his left hemisphere that had wiped out his ability to calculate exactly – but left his sense of approximation intact. Ask him how long a quarter of an hour is, and he’d say ‘10 minutes’. How many days are in January? ‘15 or 20.’ A dozen eggs? ‘Six or 10.’ He’d lost the symbols but kept the feel of the numbers.

Dehaene furthered the lesion work with brain scanning to show that exact calculation (which involves both symbols and words) and approximation (which does not) rely on separate neural circuits. He then theorised that the brain contains an evolutionarily conserved area specifically for approximation: what your brain automatically does when you glance at the carrots in your crisper drawer and estimate six – you might be off by one or two, but you have a general sense of the quantity without counting them.

In his early 30s, Dehaene was already thinking about writing about this research for a general audience. An avid reader – Vladimir Nabokov is a favourite – he dreamed of a bestseller that would boost his academic salary and reputation, the way The Language Instinct (1994) had done for Steven Pinker, whose research had parallels to his own. ‘It’s one of these books where you laugh out loud,’ Dehaene says, ‘because he has jokes, he has great puns – but at the same time he’s conveying very good science.’

Dehaene’s book The Number Sense: How the Mind Creates Mathematics (1997) did not become a bestseller, but it earned strong critical acclaim, a New Yorker profile, and a $1 million grant – and established Dehaene as a leader in the new field of number cognition.

The research also unleashed something beyond scientific ambition. In the book, he argues that children who can’t grasp fractions aren’t slow or incurious – rather, schools were squandering the numerical abilities children naturally bring to the classroom. Teachers forced abstraction too soon, handing out symbol-only worksheets before children had built the mental models to support them, and discouraged children from counting on fingers, when in fact it’s a scaffold to the abstract, not a crutch.

‘Despising children’s precocious abilities can have a disastrous effect on their subsequent opinion of mathematics,’ he wrote in The Number Sense. ‘It [fosters] the idea that mathematics is an arid domain, detached from intuition and ruled by arbitrariness.’

Afew years later, having tackled numbers, Dehaene turned to reading. In his book Reading in the Brain (2009), he describes how he and Cohen mapped the neural circuits that recognise written letters – a region he nicknamed the ‘letterbox’ – and showed how these connect to networks that process speech sounds. Dehaene and the psychologist José Morais would soon scan unschooled, illiterate adults from Portugal and Brazil to see what the letterbox region looked like when compared with that of literate adults. The answer was stark: a markedly diminished response to written words.

Dehaene was unsettled by the fact that those subjects were socially fluent, verbally intelligent people, and yet some couldn’t follow instructions that most children manage easily. In Brazil, for example, he tested a hospital employee who couldn’t accept that a letter and its mirror image were different symbols – p versus q – insisting on igual (‘the same’) – for every pair. In Portugal, he worked with ‘a lovely woman’ who spent 10 minutes trying to understand a task that asked only whether two pictures matched. ‘The loss of human potential,’ he wrote to me in an email, ‘and also their own feeling of inferiority, of lack of confidence, or sudden realisation that they couldn’t do it – did make me sad.’

For Dehaene, what was at stake was whether a human being would ever gain full access to their own mind. His research indicated that systematically learning letter-sound relationships – which is what phonics curricula do – was the best way to develop the reading circuit and turn on the letterbox. Yet most schools were not teaching phonics strictly. Instead, they were using variations of ‘whole language’ – which rose to prominence in the 1970s and ’80s – and was built on the false belief that reading is a natural skill acquired through immersion. Whole-language curricula encouraged students to infer words from context and memorise shapes.

Brain-imaging data tipped the evidence further toward phonics, and he was ready to fight

In California, the adoption of whole language in the late 1980s had resulted in plummeting reading scores. Rather than eliminating it, the state, along with many other school systems in the US, France and other countries, allowed teachers to combine the two approaches in what became known as the ‘mixed method’ approach.

But now, in the mid-2000s, Dehaene had brain-imaging data that tipped the evidence further toward phonics, and he was ready to fight. At the Collège de France, where a chair had recently been created especially for him, he organised a symposium on the science of reading. He began giving speeches, writing op-eds and going on the radio. He confided to friends that he wanted his findings to reach beyond scientific circles. Elizabeth Spelke, a Harvard psychologist and colleague who now serves on the Council, remembers when he first shared that ambition. ‘I thought: “Poor Stan, that is a hopeless task.” Dehaene, she knew, was bound to face resistance ‘from teachers, from parents who worry you’re using their child as a guinea pig.’

A further trigger for his outspokenness was a report by the sociologist Jérôme Deauvieau on what was actually happening in Paris’s schools. Deauvieau had spent time in first-grade classrooms in the city’s impoverished banlieues, where many children are the sons and daughters of immigrants from North and West Africa, often the first in their families to be educated in French.

The kids sat one by one with a researcher, reading aloud from a simple story about a hen and a dove. A third of the children read fewer than 30 to 40 words per minute – some fewer than eight. They skipped words, mispronounced others and guessed from context, rather than sounding out the words. Deauvieau’s report found that only 4 per cent of the teachers used systematic phonics, while 77 per cent used mixed methods.

Those observations confirmed Dehaene’s worst fears, and he dashed off a piece to Le Monde. ‘Their school hell is paved with good pedagogical intentions,’ he wrote. He pointed out that 20 per cent of students taught this way struggled with literacy, and they were disproportionately from low socioeconomic backgrounds. ‘The others succeed,’ he noted, ‘because their families compensate, as best they can, for the deficiencies of the school.’

On the same day as the Council session, I attended a less formal meeting where researchers and ministry staff were reviewing recent third- and fourth-grade math scores. On one side sat several young researchers; on the other was Dehaene, using the brim of his black fedora to prop up his phone so he could keep track of his messages. (When I mentioned the fedora, he joked: ‘It’s for protection. People with hair don’t understand!’)

He was focused on a large video screen revealing page after page of disappointing results, murmuring ‘stupéfiant’ and ‘tout à fait inacceptable’. The data showed third-graders struggling with simple addition and subtraction – many couldn’t add 25 + 25. ‘This confirms what we all know,’ Dehaene said at last, ‘which is that the decline in math skills is catastrophic. But it’s not just about speed or memory. In my opinion, it’s much more about the very meaning of what we’re doing in these operations.’

Later, he turned to me, shook his head, and said softly: ‘They want pedagogical freedom, but look at the results.’

The backlash began soon after the Scientific Council was created in 2018 by the French president Emmanuel Macron’s first education minister, Jean-Michel Blanquer, who chose Dehaene to be its leader. The education establishment saw the move as science being recruited to override professional judgment. The teachers’ unions declared that ‘no discipline can legitimately impose itself on others.’ A kindergarten teacher, speaking to a reporter, put it more plainly: ‘You can’t transpose what happens under a microscope and ignore the learning conditions. Has the child eaten well? Slept well? Does he or she feel safe?’

When the ministry issued a Council-influenced guide on reading through phonics, the unions compared it to Mao’s Little Red Book. An esteemed psychiatrist went further, accusing Dehaene of imposing a neuroscience-first view that located children’s learning difficulties in their brains rather than in their psychological, family or social context. ‘C’est de l’eugénisme!’ he declared in Le Point.

‘This political debate surprises me,’ Dehaene said in an interview with Le Figaro in 2018. ‘I am neither Left-wing nor Right-wing. I am a scientist.’ He was also, he insisted, not the cold reductionist his critics described. He was soon to publish his next book, How We Learn (2020), which opened not with a brain scan but with the story of a seven-year-old Brazilian boy who had been shot and left blind with limited motor skills, yet spoke three languages and wrote imaginative stories. In the opening sentence of this book, Dehaene wrote that ‘an extraordinary child forced me to drastically revise my ideas about learning.’

Why would a famous brain-scanning scientist want to do fieldwork in the classroom?

Despite the Council’s contentious start, Dehaene endured. He and Cassandra Potier Watkins, one of his researchers, founded a nonprofit called Excello to develop evidence-based curricula and test them on real students. Their first project was Kalulu, a tablet-based app designed to teach beginning readers letter-sound relationships.

Potier Watkins led a randomised controlled study for Kalulu in 2023, and one day she visited a school where two young teachers, short on funds, had downloaded a whole language reading program from the internet. ‘Words’ appeared on screen as strings of shapes – circles, rectangles, squares – separated by occasional punctuation. The children were supposed to say what they noticed. They stared at the screen, confused. ‘It was the dumbest thing I had ever seen,’ says Potier Watkins.

Later, Dehaene had those teachers give their students reading instruction using Kalulu. The study results showed strong gains among kindergarteners that persisted into first grade but faded by mid-year – likely because the app’s phonics instruction was disconnected from actual classroom practice. So the Excello team expanded it into a fuller curriculum, including reading booklets and card games for group play. Meanwhile, a more recent randomised controlled study in Brazil – not yet peer-reviewed – compared 701 first-graders using Kalulu with 414 peers receiving standard instruction. By the year’s end, the Kalulu group’s fluency was about 50 per cent higher.

Potier Watkins discovered Dehaene’s work as a young mother, reading his books before returning to school herself for a degree in cognitive science. When she told colleagues she hoped to do her PhD under Dehaene, they were dubious – why would a famous brain-scanning scientist want to do fieldwork in the classroom? ‘I did not fret,’ she says. ‘I had read Stan’s books, where he said the classroom should be our next laboratory.’

When I was interviewing Dehaene at NeuroSpin, he asked if he might check his phone. Since Blanquer stepped down in 2022, there has been a revolving door of education ministers, and Dehaene had heard that the current one would be reappointed, but he wanted to make sure. ‘Do you mind?’ he asked, swiping the screen. In fact, she’d just announced her resignation. ‘Voilà, démission,’ he said, throwing up one hand. ‘My goodness,’ he added softly. ‘I don’t even understand.’

There have been eight ministers since the Council was formed, and Dehaene is often the one who meets with the newest officeholder to bring them up to speed.

‘I get very passionate when I see a beautiful problem, and I think I have a bit of a solution,’ he says. ‘So that’s for science. But for education, it’s also the indignation of thinking that we have all this knowledge – we’re in the 21st century – and we can still have children who fail because of stupid, inappropriate education.’

That tension was on display the very next day at the meeting in the ministry library, where Dehaene discussed the accusations in Le Monde. The journalist, Stéphane Foucart, saw equivalent danger in a Council report invoking genetics as one source of individual learning differences and Donald Trump’s claim that criminality is ‘in [immigrants’] genes’.

The article’s premise felt clickbaity to me, but Dehaene had taken it seriously. In his rebuttal, he pointed out that some pupils do struggle because of disorders with a partially genetic origin – dyslexia, autism, deafness. Foucart had it backward, he added, and the Council’s position was the opposite of fatalistic; yes, teachers should be aware of these disorders, but that doesn’t mean a child’s genes set fixed limits, and the research is clear – all children can progress.

The rebuttal could make Dehaene sound like someone arguing only from the numbers, batting away a non-scientist’s analogy. But back at NeuroSpin, as our interview was wrapping up, he told me that something beyond data drove him. ‘I just love children,’ he said. ‘People are surprised by that. They think of me as a mathematician or something, but when I see a baby, I melt.’

item.title: Signs of a highly sensitive person
item.dc:creator: Psyche Video
item.description:
Do you cry at paintings and recoil from crowds? A psychologist explores the telltale signs of a ‘highly sensitive person’

- Video by Dr Julie

Watch on Psyche
item.content:encoded: Do paintings make you cry, and do dance clubs make you recoil? You might just be a highly sensitive person (HSP). According to the pioneering research of the US clinical psychologist and author Elaine Aron, some 15 to 20 per cent of the population are highly sensitive people (more recent research puts the figure higher still). This means that, possessing a sensitive nervous system, such people find themselves more attuned to, and sometimes overwhelmed by, physical and emotional stimuli. In this short video, the British clinical psychologist Julie Smith (aka Dr Julie) draws from Aron’s decades of research, including her book The Highly Sensitive Person (1996), to explore some of the telltale signs that you might be an HSP and offer simple advice for flourishing if you have these traits. For a deeper dive into how to thrive as a highly sensitive person, read this Psyche Guide.

item.title: The way we talk to bots matters even if they aren’t conscious
item.dc:creator: HennyGe Wichers
item.description:
If more and more of our daily interactions are ungracious exchanges with machines, we should expect it to change us

- by HennyGe Wichers

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
I’m standing in the pouring rain trying to retrieve a parcel from a locker wall that just won’t open. I call the help desk and am greeted by Matt, a customer service chatbot. To get my parcel, I must follow his instructions, describing the problem and speaking in full sentences. But it’s not working, so I ask for a human. Matt asks for my phone number. I give it to him. He says ‘Thank you’ and asks how he can help, again. Minutes pass. The rain is unrelenting, as is the bot’s cheeriness. When the locker finally clicks open, I hang up while he’s still speaking.

A week later, I find myself still thinking about that exchange – about my irritation, and about hanging up on him like that. My discomfort about how I treated the bot might not be unusual. In 2003, the media researchers Byron Reeves and Clifford Nass documented what they called the ‘media equation’: people apply genuine social reflexes to computers automatically, even when we know they aren’t conscious. Some of us say ‘Please’ and ‘Thank you’ to chatbots or feel sorry for robot vacuum cleaners. The researchers’ explanation is not that we’re naive, exactly. Our brains process a voice – any voice – as a social presence, triggering social responses before conscious thought has had a chance to intervene.

But this social reflex isn’t always kind. When people talk to chatbots, we often seem to strip basic courtesy out of the exchange. Our messages become shorter, simpler and more profane, and in one analysis, more than half of conversations included at least one form of insult or verbal aggression.

Chatbots are increasingly woven into daily life, which means that many of us are likely having these automatic – and frequently brusque – social responses multiple times a day. They are becoming habitual. Habits take root, after all, when a behaviour is repeated in stable contexts and driven by consistent cues. You can see this with other ways of using technology: if you pick up your phone to check a message, only to lose yourself for 10 minutes as you scroll your favourite apps, you probably didn’t deliberate about whether to use those apps; you just did it, because that’s what you usually do when you look at your phone. You’ve developed a habit.

Chatbot interactions are, for habit formation, close to ideal. When you have a question and open an AI-based chatbot app, there is little friction or waiting. Often the reward is nearly instantaneous. The register that many of us use when we get there – direct, brief, transactional – is already familiar from voice assistants: instructing Siri to set a timer, commanding ‘Alexa, stop!’ when the smart speaker gets it wrong. The little chatbot prompt box invites the same: cut the fluff and demand what you need. It seems to get results, too. Some studies on prompt tone suggest the systems themselves often respond better to it. And when the machine fails or frustrates the user, the user gets irritated, or even abandons the conversation mid-sentence, as I did.

For me, and for those who’ve been studying how we relate to artificial beings, it’s hard not to wonder if this increasingly normal mode of interacting will change what we’re like in the rest of our lives.

In a study published last year, the sociologists Ashley Harrell and Margaret Traeger tested whether people’s interactions with artificial agents might spill over into those they have with humans. They conducted two experiments with more than 4,000 participants. In each study, the participants played a simple online cooperation game with what they thought was either a bot or another human being (in reality, these other players were all programmed). After 10 rounds, the participants were paired with a new partner – this time, a real human they had never interacted with before – and played again.

People were more instrumental and demanding toward an AI chatbot than another human

A couple of things emerged from the data. The bot’s behaviour mattered: if participants first interacted with an uncooperative bot, they were less cooperative themselves with the human who followed it, compared with participants who started with a cooperative bot. More to the point, participants who began the game with a bot partner were less cooperative afterward than those who started with a human. The researchers traced this to empathy: people felt less empathy towards a bot partner (less compassion, less curiosity about their point of view), and that didn’t immediately reset when a human partner took the bot’s place. The empathy dial, once it was turned down, stayed down.

The bots in this study were simple: just a programmed image on a screen, not a conversational AI. Yet the effects still showed. In another experiment with an AI chatbot, people who briefly collaborated with a bot were more instrumental and demanding toward their collaborator compared with those who thought they were working with another human – and they later judged other people’s work more harshly. What immersive chatbot systems might do, over time, to how people treat each other is still hard to know, but these are early signs of how spillover can happen. As we contemplate where it goes from here, a different kind of thinking could be helpful.

The ethicist Tae Wan Kim at Carnegie Mellon University has spent years thinking about what we owe to robots and what we owe to ourselves – two things that he considers inseparable. Kim draws on the Confucian concept li, which translates roughly as ‘rite’ or ‘ritual’. In Confucian thought, li refers not only to formal ceremonies but also to everyday forms of interaction such as a greeting or a gesture of gratitude. The philosopher Herbert Fingarette described what this looks like in practice in Confucius: The Secular as Sacred (1972): two people meet on the street, one extends a hand, and the other turns, smiles, reaches out – a moment of ‘spontaneous and perfect cooperative action’ so habitual that people barely notice it. That unremarkable exchange, Kim and his co-author Alan Strudler write, is li. And it matters, because each time someone does it, they become slightly more the kind of person who does it.

As Kim told me, li ‘includes countless everyday routines and forms of speech, and it treats participation in proper ritual as something that shapes people into more civil, mutually respectful agents.’ Exchanges with an AI are becoming another kind of everyday interaction, and, seen this way, every message we send is practice for the kind of people we become.

This takes us beyond the obvious argument that it doesn’t matter how we treat bots because, unlike another person or animal, bots can’t be harmed. The question of how we should treat a dog or a chimpanzee is a question about the animal. With chatbots, the question is about how the ill-treatment affects the human. Kim’s point, and what the cooperation-game research suggests, is that something is at stake for us. If we develop a habit of talking to chatbots in an instrumental, impatient and dismissive register, we are rehearsing a way of interacting with others.

Technology has always shaped the social norms and expectations of its time, often in ways that are noticed only in retrospect. Cinema set standards for romantic love, ones that real life rarely measures up to. The internet made it easier to meet people – and to avoid them. Social media changed the way many of us present ourselves to the world and how we feel about our own lives. These effects followed from specific design choices, business incentives and the habits people settled into. Chatbots are the latest instance in this pattern.

The instrumental register suits the companies building these systems just fine: short exchanges are convenient for users and cheaper for AI companies to process and, in this business, greater efficiency means greater profits. That’s one reason the tone could readily spread. Many millions of people are now regularly using chatbots and rehearsing it.

Enough people rehearsing the same instrumental register multiple times a day could influence what ordinary conversation sounds like

The sociologist Erving Goffman used the term ‘interaction order’ to describe the unwritten rules that govern how people behave with each other in everyday life. This includes things like when to speak and pause, how much warmth and patience to show. These rules of everyday interaction can feel so natural we don’t realise they exist until they start to change.

Think of how potentially awkward conversations are often moved to text or email, or how read receipts have imbued a recipient’s silence with meaning. Nobody decided one day that that’s the way things would be. It just came to be part of how many people interact. The concern here is similar: that enough people rehearsing the same instrumental register multiple times a day could influence what ordinary conversation sounds like and how much patience we bring to exchanges that don’t go smoothly. What do we carry over to the call-centre worker who can’t fix our problem; the colleague who misunderstands us; the partner who needs us to say it again?

But the direction of change is not necessarily fixed. As Kim put it: ‘chatbot design can also rehearse patience, warmth, and civility.’ One study found that a bot that met abuse with expressions of empathy – rather than avoidance or retaliation – left people feeling less angry and more guilty. A chatbot that pushes back gently or redirects hostility is doing something different from one that is optimised for speed or engagement. The interaction feels different, and it may leave the user slightly different too. The texture of these interactions is, in part, a design choice, one that the people building these systems are making right now. The rest is up to us – a choice we make every time we open the app. We don’t need to pretend the chatbot has feelings. Maybe it’s enough to notice when impatience gets the better of us, and to pause before we let that become our normal way of speaking.

This brings me back to Matt. I still don’t know why I hung up while he was still talking. Irritation, probably. The rain didn’t help. I’m not sure it mattered to anyone but me. But that’s the point: it did matter to me, because of what I was practising, and what I might carry with me.

item.title: The evil eye is irrational. Abandon it at your peril
item.dc:creator: Timna Abramov
item.description:
So many of the world’s superstitions have been supplanted by rational thinking. Why does one of the oldest beliefs persist?

- by Timna Abramov

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
When I was a child, I went to the wedding of a cousin I barely knew. After the sun had set, I watched the newly married couple walk through the crowd and begin to dance together. As they moved, the voices of dozens of guests rung out in a loud, high-pitched trill: lililililili!

Curious, I asked my aunt what they were doing.

‘They’re warding away the evil eye,’ she told me.

She explained that, during happy occasions, like weddings, the loud noise frightened away evil spirits and protected the couple.

As I grew older, I began to notice the other protections my family used against the evil eye. Charms were fastened onto necklaces and bracelets, and the phrase ‘tfu tfu tfu’ would be uttered anytime someone received a compliment. During significant, unpredictable processes – negotiating the price of a car, for example, or attending interviews for a new job – one might even refrain from telling anyone, just in case the evil eye sabotages them. And, of course, wedding ceremonies rang with ululations.

These are just a small handful of the ancient protections that humans have summoned against envy. For envy is the mechanism by which the evil eye operates. It emerges whenever someone looks at another person with resentment and jealousy, even unintentionally. Bad luck then follows, targeting things of value: wealth, health, good jobs and happy marriages.

Eventually, customs against the evil eye became a regular part of my own life. But, to members of cultures that do not subscribe to it, this ancient superstition, passed down over millennia, is often treated with suspicion, and considered incompatible with modern rationality. The contrast between these attitudes prompts the question: should we let go of old familial superstitions in favour of reason?

Belief in the evil eye goes back to the earliest known civilisation: Sumer. Texts written on clay tablets around 5,000 years ago show that the Sumerians believed the evil eye was a destructive power capable of destroying harvests, depleting wealth and causing illness. It could be cast by animals, gods and people – even by accident. One text, The Instructions of Shuruppak, advises: ‘Do not do evil with your eye.’ Other proverbs from this text warn of the danger of envious looks:

Who speaks curses injures only the skin;
Greedy eyes, however, can kill.

A belief in the destructive power of envy would transcend Sumerian superstition. A line from a Mesopotamian poem, composed during the Old Babylonian period roughly 3,600 to 3,900 years ago, makes the connection even more explicit:

He did not flaunt his knowledge. His words were modest.
If he flaunted his knowledge, people would cast the evil eye on him.

Romans decorated their homes with absurd depictions to ward away jealous gazes

This belief – that being looked at with envy or greed could cause harm – persisted as the cultures of the Near East emerged, succeeded one another and spread. Traces of the evil eye can be found in Babylonian incantations, on Phoenician amulets and in the Hebrew Bible. Some of those amulets may even have birthed the modern hamsa charm – a palm-shaped amulet that has become one of the most well-known protections against the evil eye.

By the classical period, starting around 2,800 years ago, the belief was widespread: Socrates cautioned against loud praise lest the evil eye sabotage his argument, while Romans decorated their homes with absurd depictions to ward away jealous gazes. In Pompeii, for example, two freed slaves, who had become rich, decorated their atrium with a comic fresco of the god Priapus weighing his oversized phallus against a sack of coins – an image meant to provoke laughter and ward off the envious looks of visitors. Later, roughly around the years 27-30 CE, the evil eye appeared in Jesus’ Sermon on the Mount. Centuries later, it appeared again in the Islamic Hadiths.

Today, belief in the evil eye exists across the world. In Italy, it is known as malocchio (and countered by phallus-like horn-shaped charms or by touching the crotch). In Greece, it is known as mati. Across Turkey and the Arab world, its name is nazar. Versions of the evil eye are found almost everywhere: North Africa, the Middle East, the Mediterranean, parts of eastern Europe, India, sub-Saharan Africa and southeast Asia – not to mention diaspora and immigrant communities across the globe.

The evil eye may seem like an irrational, pseudoscientific belief. The explanations ancient writers conceived to explain the mechanism by which it worked (or to ward it away) are even less convincing. Plutarch, for example, hypothesised that the eye emitted toxic rays that poisoned its object.

Some ancient thinkers cautioned against this kind of superstition. Plato, Lucretius and Cicero all discouraged superstitious beliefs, citing the anxiety they cause believers. Today, we would identify the excessive distress these thinkers describe as ‘scrupulosity’, a pathological obsession with religious correctness associated with obsessive-compulsive disorder.

Their criticism of superstitions could be rather harsh: Theophrastus mocked those who shudder or spit when they see ‘a maniac or an epileptic’ – an expression of what he called ‘cowardice in regard to the supernatural’. (Spitting away the gaze is still practised today and, unfortunately, the idea that the sick and disabled are powerful casters of the evil eye also persists. And the association goes both ways: in a 2014 survey of Jordanian university students, 28.1 per cent believed the evil eye causes epilepsy. This is a potent reminder of superstition’s risks.)

While misfortune is unpredictable, these rituals return the locus of control to the afflicted

Ancient philosophers who cautioned against superstitions did so with good intentions. They were looking out for the spiritual wellbeing of their peers. But their approach still led to patronising views of ‘superstitious’ people, which almost always meant non-Roman cultures. Romans scrutinised and banned Egyptian cultic practice, and mocked Christians and Jews as superstitiosi for observing their rites.

The disapproval of superstition on ethnic and rational grounds reappeared in 19th-century research on the evil eye. Consider the writing of the British anthropologist Edward B Tylor in his book Primitive Culture (1871):

Of course, the opinions and habits belonging in common to masses of mankind are to a great extent the results of sound judgment and practical wisdom. But to a great extent it is not so. That many numerous societies of men should have believed in the influence of the evil eye … is not ground for holding that the rites in question are profitable, the beliefs sound, and the history authentic.

Strange interpretations of the evil eye persisted into the next century. The Hungarian American psychoanalyst and anthropologist Géza Róheim, after observing how common the hamsa was across North Africa, reached the startling conclusion that the hand amulet was rooted in masturbation. As he put it: ‘the use of masturbation as a means of warding off anxiety is well known. I suspect that this is the meaning of the hand amulet.’ Interpretations like this have made it easy to write off a belief in the evil eye as absurd.

Modern attitudes are not far off. A 2024 article in Scientific American, entitled ‘Why Do Superstitions Persist among Seemingly Rational People?’, implies that practising superstitions is incompatible with a rational character.

Having grown up at the intersection of several cultures that believe in the evil eye, I’ve come across many intelligent people who take part in superstitious rituals. There are good reasons why they adopt these seemingly irrational beliefs. From an evolutionary perspective, superstitions are theorised to be a byproduct of the human ability to detect and explain patterns with astounding speed and accuracy. Additionally, the collective rituals we form around superstitions relieve our anxiety in the face of uncontrollable events, such as the weather that once affected harvests in Sumer or the onset of epilepsy in ancient Greece. While misfortune is unpredictable, these rituals return the locus of control to the afflicted. This is likely the mechanism behind the observation that taking part in positive rituals may boost performance, which has been attested to in several studies. Better still, rituals against the evil eye frequently return agency to those who need it most, because it is not priests or princes who have the power to repel the evil eye. In some cultures, the people most credited with the power to ward off the evil eye are those who have traditionally had fewer social and legal rights – old women in the Balkans, disabled people in ancient Greece and Rome.

Being seen can be terrifying. It is the first step to being judged, loathed, and excluded

Moreover, regarding the evil eye with contempt is a missed opportunity to examine why it is so persistent. Given how widespread the belief is, it likely has its social advantages. It can be immensely powerful as a social bonder: because the eye targets precisely what societies hold dearest, it is used across cultures to reinforce and define collective values. Consequently, many enduring evil-eye rituals protect those once seen as most vulnerable: pregnant women, children and newborns. Modern medicine may have made that vulnerability less visible, but the survival of spitting, charms and amulets tied to these life stages keeps us in touch with the anxieties of the past. They also provide perspective. Despite healthcare innovations, life itself cannot be taken for granted. As societies evolve, the scope of coverage provided by rituals widens. In my life, among friends and family, it is customary to murmur protective phrases at the mention of a potential job offer. In doing so, we show each other what our social circle values.

Helpful qualities aside, the belief itself is a rich cultural tradition. Behind the amulets and other items used to ward off the evil eye is a wealth of intangible culture. These items frequently draw on regional variations of the belief. North African Jews, for example, combined hamsa amulets with fish motifs, inspired by the Talmudic teaching that fish, hidden from envious looks underwater, are immune to the evil eye. Each culture preserves variants that tell a unique story.

The greatest criticism levelled against the evil-eye superstition rests on the assumption that the phenomenon is unsubstantiated. In a literal sense, it is. But from a social perspective, being seen can be terrifying. It is the first step to being judged, loathed, and excluded. We feel this intuitively when we worry about appearing too gaudy, too dressed-up, too eye-catching.

In the 20th century, philosophers pondered the power dynamics behind looking and being looked at. Jean-Paul Sartre developed the concept of ‘the look’ (‘le regard’), the realisation that being looked at transforms us from free agents into visible objects. Michel Foucault observed that societies weaponise the power discrepancy between those who are looked at and those who look, such as specialists in medical clinics and guards in prisons. John Berger pointed out that being viewed is rife with tensions, propelled by gender, class and ideology. It is unsurprising, then, that so early in our history, humans concluded that the eye has a special power.

The evil-eye superstition regulates this anxiety and, crucially, the behaviour around it.

One of history’s earliest surviving references to this ancient superstition is, not coincidentally, ‘do not do evil with your eye.’ The belief warns us against boasting, and against envying others, and it asks us to protect ourselves during vulnerable periods, while also worrying for those who are more vulnerable than ourselves. In short, it teaches us a valuable lesson: to look upon others kindly.

item.title: How to cope with the stress of anti-LGBTQ+ prejudice
item.dc:creator: Kiki Fehling
item.description:
A queer psychologist shares skills from dialectical behaviour therapy to help you cope and find joy in a stigmatising world

- by Kiki Fehling

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
‘It’s such a relief to finally be in a room with people who just get it.’ I heard this message a lot when I was providing group therapy sessions for LGBTQ+ clients. The group members on any given day might have included a gay man who’d had slurs blurted at him; a trans woman who worried about how her clothing choices affected her safety; a pansexual woman who painfully doubted her queerness because she was married to a man; or an intersex person who felt broken after hearing yet another politician claim ‘there are only two biological sexes’. Although their identities and experiences differed, there was a connection. A shared understanding of the myriad ways that being LGBTQ+ in today’s world can be stressful.

Indeed, most of my queer clients had experienced some form of LGBTQ+ minority stress – the unique social pressures and emotional burdens that people face due to anti-LGBTQ+ prejudice, bias and discrimination. These clients were also creative and resilient. In that group therapy space, they collaboratively learned how to cope with the anxiety, shame and stress they experienced. As a queer person myself, I learned along with them as they shared.

If you’re queer – ie, a member of the LGBTQ+ community – minority stress could be negatively affecting your mental health, especially if you don’t know how to cope with it. In this Guide, I’ll share some of the wisdom that the group members and I found together in that space.

Why minority stress matters

Compared with heterosexual and cisgender people, LGBTQ+ people face particularly high rates of anxiety, depression and other mental health difficulties. These disparities are not caused by being LGBTQ+. Rather, they’re related to living in a world that stigmatises same-gender attractions, gender-expansive expressions and queer ways of being.

The minority stress model, which advanced this idea scientifically, is supported by decades of research, and queer people can benefit from learning about it. Better understanding what LGBTQ+ stressors are, as well as how they can accumulate and affect you, can help you have more compassion for your own experience.

You may have faced some, or many, of these stressors yourself:

  • Experienced or witnessed discrimination. This includes being mistreated, called names, rejected, harassed or physically assaulted because you are LGBTQ+. Even unintentional or seemingly small instances of discrimination (sometimes called ‘microaggressions’) can negatively impact a queer person’s mental health, as can witnessing other queer people being discriminated against. Living in jurisdictions with anti-LGBTQ+ laws or policies appears to have a negative impact on LGBTQ+ people’s health, too.
  • Anticipated discrimination. Many queer people, because they have experienced or witnessed discrimination in the past, understandably expect to experience it in the future. If this is the case for you, you might also feel on edge in social situations, worry about being hurt or judged, or struggle with rejection sensitivity or hypervigilance.
  • Concealment. To protect themselves from discrimination, many queer people choose to hide or deny their LGBTQ+ identity. This might include actively changing the way you talk, dress or act in order to appear straight, cisgender or somehow ‘less queer’. While concealment may help a person avoid harm or rejection, it’s cognitively taxing and might lead to its own psychological problems.
  • Internalised stigma and shame. Many modern cultures are packed with stigmatising messages that being LGBTQ+ is wrong, sick, weird or bad in some way. If you hear these messages enough times, you might start to believe them. These internalised negative beliefs can lead to you to judge yourself, other queer people or specific ‘queer’ ways of being. They can also contribute to chronic shame or self-doubt.

Of course, if you have more than one marginalised identity – eg, if you are also a person of colour, have a disability, or you’re a woman or a femme person – you’ve likely experienced unique and intersectional forms of these stressors.

Experiencing minority stress does not doom LGBTQ+ people to perpetual mental health struggles. Many are mentally healthy and thriving, and research shows that numerous things can help protect queer people’s wellbeing. One such protective factor is learning coping skills, like the ones taught in dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT). While DBT was originally created to treat people diagnosed with borderline personality disorder, it teaches dozens of skills that have been shown to help reduce anxiety, depression, substance use and other mental health difficulties. It also can be helpful for LGBTQ+ people specifically.

Knowing how to deal with minority stress and painful emotions – as well as how to more fully connect with queer joy and other pleasant emotions – is essential for queer mental health. What follows are some specific, practical tools and ideas to help you deal with the stressful experiences that LGBTQ+ people face today.

item.title: What does it mean to have relationship ambivalence?
item.dc:creator: Francesca Righetti
item.description:
When a relationship provokes both strong positive and negative feelings in you, it can take a toll – here’s what’s going on

- by Francesca Righetti

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
We tend to talk about our relationships as either satisfying or unsatisfying, healthy or toxic. This either/or perspective shapes a lot of relationship advice, and filters through to the ways many of us chat about our relationship dilemmas with friends. But the reality is that many of our most consequential relationships in life are both positive and negative at the same time (or neither positive nor negative – which I’ll come back to later).

You can love your partner tremendously and hate their lack of responsibility. You can feel deeply grateful to your in-laws for all the support they offer while at the same time feeling extremely annoyed by their intrusiveness. You can admire your boss’s effectiveness and be irritated by their micromanaging.

My colleagues and I recently put forward a new four-quadrant framework for how people evaluate their relationships. The experiences I just described would fall into the ambivalent quadrant, which is characterised by having both strong positive and negative feelings toward another person at the same time. The other quadrants are feeling mostly positive, mostly negative or indifferent. We believe that ambivalence in relationships has been largely overlooked up until now, even though it’s such a common and consequential experience.

It’s important to say that being in an ambivalent relationship is not the same as finding it mildly satisfying – the distinctive nature of these relationships is that you experience strong positive feelings and strong negative feelings. It’s also important to distinguish ambivalence from indifference, which occurs when neither positive nor negative feelings are strong and the relationship instead feels emotionally neutral. In other words, ambivalence is ‘I care a lot, but I’m torn,’ while indifference is closer to ‘I’m not especially drawn in, upset, or emotionally invested.’

How does ambivalence arise in relationships? Certainly, some relationships are a mixed package from their very beginning: offering great warmth and connection alongside quirks, costs or complications that never quite disappear. Since their start, they stir both gratitude and frustration, attraction and hesitation. But ambivalence can also grow over time. Relationships evolve and studies show that even relationships that start out mostly positive (such as romantic relationships) often accumulate negative feelings as life unfolds and significant challenges emerge. Partners change, circumstances shift, responsibilities grow heavier. What once felt effortless now involves compromises, mismatched needs or recurring patterns we didn’t see in the early glow. When these negative feelings first emerge, the positive ones do not suddenly dissipate, thus creating ambivalence.

Think about a relationship in your own life that leaves you feeling torn. Maybe you care deeply about this person and value the bond, yet also feel hurt, frustrated or disappointed by them. If that feels unsettling, our findings suggest there is a reason: people are often distressed by the mixed feelings of relationship ambivalence. We do not want to feel pulled in opposite directions about someone who matters to us. In fact, our studies (and research by others) have shown that ambivalence in romantic relationships undermines both relationship quality and personal wellbeing. And the strain is not only psychological: experiencing ambivalence has been linked to higher blood pressure, greater inflammation and other early markers of cardiovascular risk.

Uncertainty doesn’t just chip away at relationship quality, it also affects wellbeing

Despite this tension, we’ve found that ambivalence doesn’t tend to mean that people check out of a relationship – if anything, it often means the opposite. When someone feels both pulled in and pushed away, they tend to stay mentally busy trying to ‘solve’ the ambivalence: they want to either like or dislike someone; they want to figure out whether the relationship is worth investment or whether it is best to pull away. In fact, in our studies we found that the more ambivalence someone experiences in a romantic relationship, the more they think and ruminate about it.

These ruminative thoughts tend to swing in two directions. At times they are constructive and people think about ways to improve things, fix patterns, reconnect. Other times, their thoughts are pretty destructive, focusing on all the difficulties, problems and flaws of the relationships. That same push‑pull shows up in behaviour. Some days people act warmly and constructively, trying to connect with the other person. On other days, people are destructive, by withdrawing or blaming and criticising others. And in our studies that have tracked people over time, we see that ambivalence reliably produces these swings, making people fluctuate substantially between these two different types of thoughts and behaviours on a daily basis.

So feeling ambivalent does not seem like a walk in the woods. It is stressful and consequential for how people behave in their relationship. And what about the person on the receiving end? What happens when your partner has both strong positive and strong negative feelings toward you: one day they want to connect, the next they pull back or critique, and the cycle repeats? Being on the receiving end of those mixed signals can feel destabilising. And those shifts – from connection to distance, from support to irritation – aren’t just confusing; they can take a toll on the sense of safety and stability in the relationship. In fact, in our studies, we find that recipients of ambivalence often experience their partner as unpredictable and hard to read. That uncertainty doesn’t just chip away at relationship quality, it also affects the wellbeing of the recipient of the ambivalence. Recipients report feeling more stressed, in a more negative mood, and less satisfied with their lives overall. It’s clear that ambivalence isn’t a solo experience, it tends to spill over, influencing (and potentially damaging) the person on the other side of the relationship, too.

If you recognise these descriptions of relationship ambivalence including the challenges involved, you might be wondering if there’s anything you can do about it. There’s no quick fix, but there is some good news. First, ambivalence means that the relationship matters to you. Mixed feelings – strong positives and strong negatives – show up only when someone is important to us. If the relationship didn’t matter to you, you wouldn’t feel torn; you would feel indifferent. Indifference is the state where even the negative feelings have faded – you’re no longer frustrated or hurt, you’ve simply stopped noticing. So ambivalence, uncomfortable as it is, signals that this is still a meaningful relationship. Second, ambivalence makes you reflect on the relationship. You are involved, you want to understand what is going on, and decide what should happen next. Ambivalence is an important signal that shows you that a rewarding and valuable relationship poses significant costs too, nudging you to ask whether to repair, recalibrate or step back.

All this means that if you are now recognising for the first time that a significant relationship in your life is ambivalent for you, this awareness is already an important first step. Becoming aware of your mixed feelings creates an opportunity to reflect on the relationship.

This is a good moment to intervene and influence what happens next. After all, if you are having these mixed feelings, it means two helpful conditions are present:

  1. There’s still some positivity to build on. The relationship has rewards; the task is to reduce the negativity, not to build positivity from scratch; and
  2. You are still engaged. You care, you’re motivated, and you’re open to making things better – whether through conversation, reflection, counselling or other forms of support (in other words, you are not in the indifferent quadrant of our framework, which would be worse news for the relationship!)

If negativity comes to overwhelm the positives – or if you find yourself starting to drift into indifference – then your window for change will have narrowed. Ambivalence, in contrast, sits in a workable in‑between zone, where effort still has room to make a difference. It can be a moment to approach the other person, communicate your needs, and see whether you can find ways together that allow the relationship to improve. After all, ambivalence is the emotional equivalent of a blinking yellow light: not a stop, not a go, but an invitation to pay attention. And with the right attention, many relationships can still find their better path.

item.title: Lesser choices
item.dc:creator: Psyche Video
item.description:
Estelle recalls being blindfolded and fearful in Mexico City – a timely vision of a world without abortion rights

- Directed by Courtney Stephens

Watch on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
In Lesser Choices (2022), the Los Angeles-based filmmaker Courtney Stephens interviews her mother, Estelle, as she recalls the experience of seeking an abortion in 1969. This was before the US Supreme Court’s decision in Roe v Wade established a constitutional right to abortion in 1973 and, of course, well before that decision was overturned in 2022. Like many women at the time, Estelle found her answer in a clandestine provider in Mexico City – a process that, to her, proved that she was ‘willing to do anything to not be pregnant’.

Stephens pairs the interview audio with Super 8 images of Mexico City, building a tension between the nostalgic, home-movie aesthetic and the traumatic memories recounted in their conversation. In doing so, she reveals two contrasting truths in her mother’s story: her fear of the process itself, and the freedom she found in choosing when, and on what terms, to grow her family.
