For more from Stephens, watch her short Ida Western Exile.

item.title: The softness of metal
item.dc:creator: Keith Kahn-Harris
item.description:
Watching a seated Ozzy play his final gig, my ankle broken, I’m in tears – this couldn’t be more metal

- by Keith Kahn-Harris

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
I am grateful no one else is in the room with me. In principle, I’ve no problem with my family seeing me cry: but blinking away hot salty tears while watching Ozzy Osbourne? That seems somehow ludicrous. This is, after all, the self-styled prince of darkness, a trickster-like figure – one part devil, one part joker, one part joke.

I thought I knew Ozzy – we all thought we knew him, whether we liked him or not. He was the fresh-faced, charismatic vocalist of Black Sabbath. He was the bloated, crazed, drug-addled artist who bit the head off a dead bat onstage and once tried to strangle his wife. Later in life he was the lovable, bewildered paterfamilias on The Osbournes reality TV series. For some, he was also the artist with a back catalogue on which much of metal still rests.

The Ozzy that is making me cry is none of those things.

Here I am, in the easy chair in our living room, laptop balanced on my thighs, my recently broken ankle encased in a support boot and raised up on a bolster. Weeping. My lower leg and foot prickle with heat on this sultry day in July 2025, and I cannot take my eyes off Ozzy performing the final show of his illustrious career, at Villa Park in Birmingham, UK, before an ecstatic audience, and for those like me who have paid for the live stream. There are no antics, no wide-eyed devilish grin, none of the incessant running back and forth that we’re used to from him. Instead, he sits on a bat-shaped throne, singing with an appalling intensity, and occasionally demanding that the crowd clap along.

All day long I’d been watching metal’s great and good perform brief sets in honour of the man who inspired so many of them. Grizzled veteran megastars like Metallica, emerging legends like Gojira and fresh-faced talents like Yungblud and Lzzy Hale – all of them merely support acts just for one day, playing brief sets in which Ozzy/Sabbath covers predominate. Now, finally, it’s Ozzy’s turn.

He had been waiting for this moment to say a final goodbye for years. Health problems and the COVID-19 pandemic meant he’d had to cancel most of his farewell tour. Three years on from his only stage appearance since then (a couple of songs performed at a 2022 NFL game), he is obliged to perform seated due to a litany of medical complaints: Parkinson’s disease, acute back and neck trouble, and a whole lot else. You can see that singing takes everything he has left. He wants to stand, to run, to be the embodiment of rock and roll that he once was. It’s heartbreaking.

Ozzy professes his love for us and we return it, myself included. Even viewed on a laptop screen from my own sick chair, it feels like a deluge of emotion. A surfeit of love, pain, frailty and loss are converging on my own frail body.

When I first discovered Ozzy and metal, as a child on the cusp of adolescence, metal bodies seemed like the embodiment of strength and virility. The tousled locks, the phallic guitar poses, the distortion, the screams and the implausible vibrato – all this felt like what a man should be. Metal bodies thrilled me, the more so since, as a skinny, nebbish Jew, I felt I could never inhabit one.

He was always different, pudgy, vulnerable, a ball of emotion and confusion

My Jewish North London upbringing was settled, middle class, rule bound. Metal was none of those things and nor was Ozzy. Metal was confrontation, insensitive and insouciant to the loathing and derision its artists received from the mainstream music majority. Ozzy lived a life wilfully devoted to the pursuit of shock. His music, and metal more generally, explored the darkest of themes; violence, death and suicide, the occult, all the delights of transgression.

Yet, had I looked a little deeper, I would have discovered a different Ozzy that coexisted with the one I knew; an Ozzy I might have found common ground with. Physically, he was never a metal god either. He was always different, pudgy, vulnerable, a ball of emotion and confusion, far from the image of masculine mastery. Like me, he desperately felt he had to embody metal. Like me, he frequently felt shame for the weakness of his flesh. Unlike me, he somehow became the apotheosis of metal masculinity.

I spend the week before the show suffering, after slipping down the stairs in the middle of the night. It was my daughter’s Father’s Day card that I slipped on – a metaphor I don’t even want to think about. After a couple of days hobbling around the house, I give in to reality and get an X-ray. While I am waiting for the results, my son calls to tell me he was awarded a first class in his honours degree. I yelp. Then I learn that my ankle is fractured.

I spend the day before Ozzy’s final show alternately being wheeled and limping around a university town for the ceremonial awarding of my son’s degree. It’s a luminous, barely believable day, as I remember my son’s late diagnosis of dyslexia and the educational turmoil he’d had to cope with during the pandemic.

Ozzy’s brave performance stirs an emotional pot already full to the brim

In the afterglow of these hours spent marinating in love, and as I watch Ozzy declaring his love for the crowd, I can’t entirely banish the undercurrent of guilt that never leaves me on account of another bond of love: my immobility means that I haven’t been to visit my father today, in the nursing home where he has been confined for nearly a year. Like Ozzy, my dad has Parkinson’s disease and much else; standing up is a chancy enterprise for him. This week he won’t receive the fleeting comfort of a visit from me. It was my turn to be the man, to take over from the one who once carried me. Instead, there is only my weakness.

A weak father, a weak son; immobile while watching a weak man somehow transcend his desperate situation. So I cry, as Ozzy’s brave performance stirs an emotional pot already full to the brim.

I’ve spent years studying metal as a scholar and writing about it anywhere that will publish me. I know that metal today is a more diverse place. London’s best metal pub has a vegan menu and its best metal record store has an alcohol-free bar; metal festivals have viewing platforms for people with mobility issues. Metal is even used as a resource in support groups and 12-step programmes. Yet Ozzy’s performance still shocks me into a different kind of understanding. Who knew that metal could be a place where one of its most notorious stars could perform this achingly sad display of vulnerability and yearning?

Confined to his throne-cum-prison, Ozzy clearly feels something of this unnerving surprise himself. You can tell that his frustration with his disability is tinged with a portion of shame. He loves the love he’s getting, but he can’t play the transgressive part he’s played for so long. The pathos of his evident grief, his mourning the loss of what he once was, is hard to witness.

What appears to be metallic hardness is but a patina for something else

Ozzy may have helped create heavy metal but that doesn’t mean that he fully understood his creation, its possibilities and potential. Then again, for much of metal’s history, neither did anyone else. We were all sucked into the myth that the metal men were selling, to the point where we sometimes forgot that it was a myth.

I am as old as metal is, and as I aged the genre aged too. In adulthood, as a doctoral student, academic and writer, I learned that what appears to be metallic hardness is but a patina for something else – the terrifying realisation that, as humans, we are all condemned to the dirt and to the limitations of the body. For all that metal sometimes looks like a playpen for those gripped by delusions of mythic power, at its core there is also fear, despair and brokenness.

It was always there. Hiding in plain sight in Ozzy’s work. Songs like ‘Suicide Solution’ (1980), ‘So Tired’ (1983) and ‘Mama, I’m Coming Home’ (1991) helped to make metal the sound of suffering, and of weakness. That’s true even for metal men who present outwardly as the epitome of the metal warrior. Many of the artists who played Ozzy’s farewell show had explored this territory: Metallica’s ‘Welcome Home (Sanitarium)’ (1986), Pantera’s ‘I’m Broken’ (1994), and Tool’s ‘Forty Six and 2’ (1997) burn with pain and rage.

As a scholar, I learn fast. As a person with a body and a propensity for shame and anxiety, I learn achingly slowly. I wish that, years earlier, I’d internalised what I’d learned metal could be. Like Ozzy, I too have a body that fails me on occasion (I’ve had chronic fatigue syndrome for more than 30 years). Even before that, I never much liked my gawky, ungainly body anyway: I loved metal, but felt I couldn’t be metal. I wrote about the softness at the core of the metal body long before I accepted the squishiness in my own metal bone locker. Yet like Ozzy, I was more metal than I ever could have imagined.

Something had begun to shift for me in the years preceding Ozzy’s final concert. For this male Jewish weakling, metal and shame were natural bedfellows. My children were raised to be shameless: their musical tastes and their frailties were matters of fact. They both found their way to metal with little help from me.

Metal has become the place where my body can betray me, where I can be weak

My daughter fell particularly hard for metallic art. As an autistic person, she knows about limits and excess – meat and drink to metal culture. For years now, I’ve been taking her to gigs. Most recently, as she suffered through an energy-limiting conditions in her late teens, I’ve wheeled her into the disabled section at multiple venues. Unlike Ozzy and unlike me, she was unembarrassed about sitting down. She knew that metal was an ode sung by and to and about fallible bodies. She knew she was metal.

If only Ozzy had known that, too. He knew only the contrast between what he had once tried to be and what he now was: that the monumental myth had crumbled. And I, caught between my daughter’s generation and Ozzy’s, wept tears of sadness for what he would never understand – and tears of happiness for my children’s lack of shame (mingling with tears of pain as my ankle throbbed).

I always thought I would move on from metal as I aged. The opposite happened: following my daughter’s example, metal has become the place where my body can betray me, where I can be weak, where I can acknowledge my frailty. Looking round the audience at gigs, I can see that I am not the only one who knows this.

Ozzy died just 17 days after his final concert, on 22 July 2025. This time I didn’t cry. When I heard the news, I thought ‘How perfect!’ To end one’s life this way, after a mega performance of loving and being loved, was a beautiful thing. For one night only, Ozzy became the one who could strip bare my defences and make me feel. And what a blessing it was to be immobile at the time, joining my dad, my daughter and Ozzy in that place where there is no hiding from the fact that flesh is weak.

item.title: Maxxing treats life as a problem when it’s a mystery
item.dc:creator: Håkon Evjemo
item.description:
The philosopher Gabriel Marcel offers the antidote to a grotesque new ideology: don’t fix existence, be open to it

- by Håkon Evjemo

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
In 2021, while working from home at my corporate law gig, I became obsessed with napping. Throughout my working life, the post-lunch slump felt like an unavoidable feature of the 9-to-5. Then I read Why We Sleep (2017) by Matthew Walker. It was one of a new breed of popular books that used scientific research to deepen our understanding of everyday activities. This book did two things for me. First, it justified my post-lunch nap as a way of optimising my afternoons. Second, and more importantly, it transformed what I considered to be an unavoidable feature of life into a fixable bug. Going beyond the science of sleep, it presented me with the taste of a new approach to life, one that could, if taken to the extreme, conceivably reduce my life to a series of problems amenable to practicable solutions.

Equipped with this newfound confidence in the power of solving life’s problems, I went on a reading spree. I cultivated atomic habits. I learned the Wim Hof Method. Embraced the plasticity of my own brain. Gorged on healthy fats. Cut out gluten. Lined my kitchen with jars of home-made sauerkraut.

Eating well, exercising regularly, learning new skills – these are cornerstones of many self-improvement regimes. Who would not welcome a bit of science to shed more light on how these work? This is precisely what books like Why We Sleep – as well as Atomic Habits (2018) by James Clear, Mind Your Gut (2024) by Kate Scarlata and Megan Riehl, and The Brain that Changes Itself (2007) by Norman Doidge – intend. And yet, working my way through these books I could not help but notice something more nefarious at play. This new toolkit of science-backed interventions seemed to grow into something greater than the sum of their parts. The question of the good life was devolving into a far less ambitious task: the solved life. When we fully reduce life to a series of problems in need of solutions, and when we rely exclusively on these solutions as the means to live a good life, we have succumbed to what I call the scientification of the good life.

Where might the scientification of the good life lead us? In recent years, this relatively innocuous application of science to life has curdled into something grotesque. We are now in an era of what Gen Z calls ‘maxxing’: internet slang for ruthlessly quantifying and optimising social or physiological traits in pursuit of better social standing or lifestyle. The most notable figure is Clavicular (real name Braden Eric Peters), the figurehead of ‘looksmaxxing’, a sub-genre of maxxing that urges people, usually young men, to optimise their physical proportions and facial structure to meet ideal standards. The purpose of looksmaxxing is to ‘mog’, or dominate other men by being more attractive. Common interventions include smashing the jawbone to achieve facial symmetry, self-prescribed methamphetamine to manage weight, and the injection of peptides for supposed skincare benefits.

Looksmaxxing only scratches the surface of a subculture evolving into a full-blown ideology, complete with its own market, language and devoted followers. The proliferation of other forms of maxxing – sleepmaxxing, statusmaxxing, financemaxxing, even vibemaxxing – signals its tendency to expand beyond addressing one particular aspect of life to addressing life as a whole. What fundamentally motivates maxxing is the need to take control by forcefully reducing life to a series of fixable problems. While pseudoscientific interventions like bonesmashing and mewing have taken the ‘science’ out of scientification, the underlying problem-solving attitude I got a taste of has not only remained but has been, as it were, put on steroids, bringing with it the overinflated expectation of actually solving life. Has maxxing delivered on its promises? All I have seen is an obsession with hollow values that lead to substance abuse, infertility, even incarceration. Clearly something profound is missing from the maxxing lifestyle.

If there was any figure I would nominate as a fantasy guest on a maxxer’s livestream or podcast, it would be the 20th-century Catholic existentialist Gabriel Marcel. Though born in 1889, his work reads almost like a philosophical diagnosis of the maxxing trend. Marcel mixed existentialism and phenomenology to cultivate a style of philosophising that relied on common language and everyday experience. His central preoccupation was the ‘ontological mystery’: how to remain open to existence as something we inhabit, rather than a problem to fix. His main warning to maxxers would be this: stop trying to reduce life to a series of problems in need of a fix. Learn to live it.

Hospitals, once understood as places of care, attentiveness and solidarity in the face of suffering, become repair shops

In The Philosophy of Existentialism (1956), Marcel offers a critique of modernity. It begins with a simple observation: the modern world appears broken in the way a machine appears broken. Science affords us the ability to understand how something works, to set standards of ideal function, and therefore to know when things fall short. Brokenness becomes an essential feature of this world. For Marcel, this tendency to see the world as broken eventually turns inward. We come to see ourselves as nothing more than an ‘agglomeration of functions’ (physiological, social, even economic) that adhere to scientifically determined standards amenable to restoration, preservation or enhancement.

This changes the way we approach life. Whether it’s getting your 10,000 steps in a day, cultivating a healthy relationship with your family members, or meeting your KPI’s at work, life becomes governed by what Marcel calls a ‘vital schedule’ designed to repair, regulate, even optimise these functions. Hospitals, once understood as places of care, attentiveness and solidarity in the face of suffering, become repair shops. Workplaces, once sites of vocation, craft and communal purpose, become sites of efficiency. Even my daily naps are tweaks to my own vital schedule. Marcel’s warning is that total immersion in functionality excludes something: ‘this world is, on the one hand, riddled with problems and, on the other, determined to allow no room for mystery.’

According to Marcel, this world of agglomerated functions suffers from a peculiar blindness: it mistakes mysteries for problems. Problems are detachable things we can step back from and solve. Examples include nourishing your gut microbiome after a strong course of antibiotics, navigating toxic relationships, or investing smartly to build your pension. A mystery, by contrast, is what he calls ‘a problem which encroaches upon its own data’: situations in which we are so profoundly implicated that no amount of diagnostic distance can resolve them. Life is one of these mysteries. Matthew Walker can tell me why I am tired. He cannot tell me why, after the nap, I still felt hollow working another lacklustre day drafting commercial property leases for a global pension fund. That hollowness is not a problem to be solved. It is a mystery to be inhabited. And it is precisely this distinction, between the solved life and the lived one, that pop-sci self-helpery, for all its genuine utility, papers over.

For Marcel, whether we treat life as a problem or a mystery depends on whether we adopt the style of ‘having’ or ‘being’. To ‘have’ a life is to treat life as an object I possess. To ‘be’ a life is to recognise I am profoundly implicated in it. This distinction maps onto the difference between problems and mysteries. We ‘have’ problems. A problem is something I can step outside of and inspect from a distance. Its amenability to solution is guaranteed by the fact that I am not implicated in it. It is ‘out there’, waiting to be solved by a method I bring to it. A mystery, by contrast, is something I ‘am’. I cannot step outside of it because I inhabit it, and what I inhabit cannot be diagnosed and solved from a distance. If problem-solving fails in the face of mysteries, I am forced to adopt a different style of living.

Marcel’s key observation is this: ‘having’ is always a temporary excursion from ‘being’. As Marcel puts it in Being and Having (1949), ‘having tends, not to be destroyed, but to be sublimated and changed into being.’ Like dams that break the flow of water, the act of ‘having’ involves what Marcel calls ‘a kind of suppressed dynamic’. I can posit my body as an object for me, then work on it as if it were a broken machine, but I always have to return to my body as something to live in. The dam of ‘having’ my body as something to work on always breaks. This return to being is not incidental but structural: ‘being’ sustains ‘having’, the mystery of living will always encapsulate the solving of problems.

Stop trying to perfect the system of yourself. Instead, cultivate a willingness to be surprised by your own existence

The scientification of the good life overlooks this. It promises a world of pure ‘having’, dictated entirely by diagnosing and solving problems. But the inevitable moments of return, in which the attitude of having and solving problems reverts to the mystery of being, puncture this fantasy. The life that we return to after tweaking it from afar still has to be lived, to be inhabited, and whatever this style of living is, it cannot be served by scientification. For Marcel, the maxxer’s tragedy is not that they are wrong about the value of optimisation, but that they have narrowed their existential horizon exclusively to problem-solving. Instead of trying to fix the mystery of being, maxxers should be finding ways to be at home in it.

This involves not just relinquishing control over what you cannot control, but relinquishing the very attitude of being in control. Admittedly, this is a hard sell, especially for those who believe achieving full control can lead to a good life. This is made harder by the fact that there is no ideal function of participation and therefore is no ‘How to…’ guide on how to participate in life. But to be clear, Marcel doesn’t suggest we abandon all forms of problem-solving. A sleep deficit is a problem; taking a nap solves it. His warning is that life ultimately exceeds the limits of problem-solving. The danger of scientification arises only when we mistake ‘having’ for an exclusive style of living.

Abraham Maslow’s law of the instrument suggests that, to someone with a hammer, everything looks like a nail. Marcel develops this into what we might now call a ‘law of the toolbox’: in a world shaped by techno-scientific success, everything is seen as a problem to be solved. This is an infectious style of living. But this style, effective as it is, becomes self-reinforcing and exclusive of other styles of living. For the maxxers scrolling through morning routines and biohacking protocols, Marcel offers an uncomfortable wisdom: stop trying to perfect the system of yourself. Instead, cultivate a willingness to be surprised by your own existence, to acknowledge what cannot be measured or fixed. This is not passivity. It is a deeper form of engagement. One that recognises the limits of mastery and finds meaning precisely in what escapes our control.

item.title: Go ahead, jump on the bandwagon
item.dc:creator: Hannah Seo
item.description:
Rooting for a team and other collective experiences are opportunities to be seized – even if only once in a while

- by Hannah Seo

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
I will confess that, when it comes to sports, I am a fair-weather fan. I like basketball but had little interest in the New York Knicks until they made it to the NBA finals in June. I’m barely interested in soccer unless the Canadian team or the Korean team make it at least to the World Cup round of 32. I root for teams when there’s cause to hope and, when they do advance, I’m as joyful and riotous as any fan.

My intermittent fandom used to be a source of sheepishness. It’s easy to feel, or be made to feel, like a fake fan or a poseur. Especially if you’re among ‘real’, lifelong fans. But this year, I’ve learned to embrace fair-weather fandom as a legitimate way to join in with a collective experience. While there will always be someone out there who might grumble about my fan status or try to flex their superior knowledge of player history, I’ve found that most people are just happy you’re celebrating with them – that you’ve come to recognise a team’s greatness.

Jumping on bandwagons is a normal and valuable part of life, really. We all use cues from the people around us to decide when and where to shift our attention. And if, for a brief window of time, we turn that gaze to a sports team we wouldn’t ordinarily focus on, that’s our prerogative. After all, watching sports can be really good for our psychological wellbeing – in part, research suggests, because of the social connection it promotes as we watch along with other fans. I particularly love those moments when a crowd of like-minded fans grows tense, hearts all racing together, until our team pulls through and we erupt into roars. When there’s an opportunity to participate in that shared drama and excitement, we should seize it.

item.title: A brief history of Viagra
item.dc:creator: Psyche Video
item.description:
Discovered by accident, it became the fastest-selling drug of the century. Did it revolutionise sex or reinforce old ideas?

- Video by BBC Ideas, The Open University

Watch on Psyche
item.content:encoded: In the 1990s, an otherwise unremarkable trial for a potential angina treatment ushered in a new chapter in the history of sex and sexuality. The discovery of some unexpected side effects resulted in the widespread availability of sildenafil – better known by its brand name, Viagra. In this animation, delivered with a healthy dose of bawdy humour, the UK sex educator Justin Hancock offers a brief history of the drug, which provided an effective and relatively cheap solution to the age-old issue of erectile disfunction. Further, Hancock considers the pitfalls of the little blue pill, including the concern that other potential uses of sildenafil have been under-studied and sidelined, and that it’s boosted some unhelpful ideas about sex and masculinity.

item.title: Terminal lucidity: when dying dementia patients regain awareness
item.dc:creator: Ariel Zeleznikow-Johnston
item.description:
The reports span centuries and cultures. If they’re real, memory and identity might be far more recoverable than we thought

- by Ariel Zeleznikow-Johnston

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
An 81-year-old woman with advanced Alzheimer’s is living in a retirement home in Iceland. She hasn’t recognised her family or spoken a word to them in a year. One day, while her son Lydur is sitting beside her working on a crossword puzzle, she sits up and looks him directly in the face.

‘My Lydur,’ she says. ‘I am going to recite a verse to you.’

And then she says the following in a loud and clear voice:

Oh, father of light, be adored.
Life and health you gave to me,
My father and my mother.
Now I sit up, for the sun is shining.
You send your light in to me.
Oh, God, how good you are.

She then lies back down and never talks again. In a month, she dies.

This case, reported in a 2011 study by the biologist Michael Nahm and colleagues from the University of Virginia and the University of Iceland, is an example of terminal lucidity: an unexpected return of cognitive function in patients with severe dementia (or other brain damage) that occurs shortly before death.

As a neuroscientist, my first thoughts when encountering reports like this are that they can’t possibly be real. The main reason is that, by the time patients with severe dementia die, their brains are catastrophically damaged. For a protracted period before death, these patients typically show no signs of recognising family members. They often haven’t responded meaningfully to their environment in months or years. And they’ve lost 20 to 50 per cent of their synaptic connections – so much that their brains have visibly shrunk on MRI scans.

On top of this existing damage, the dying process itself is hardly optimal for brain function. Everything we know about neuroscience says this should make cognition worse, not better.

And yet, terminal lucidity keeps being reported.

If a dying brain can spontaneously access ‘lost’ memories, perhaps we could induce a living brain to do the same

In some reports, 60 to 70 per cent of dementia caregivers say they’ve witnessed at least one patient return to lucidity in the days before death. In a study that specifically followed deaths in hospice, researchers found examples of terminal lucidity in 6 per cent of cases. That makes the phenomenon neither ubiquitous nor rare – in the US alone, it would mean around 10,000 cases per year.

This potentially has profound implications for neuroscience and medicine.

Retaining memories depends on neural circuitry maintaining specific synaptic connection strengths. As dementia progresses, memory worsens because these neural structures physically deteriorate – synapses disintegrate, neurons die. So when a woman who hasn’t recognised her son in a year suddenly calls him by name and recites a poem she learned during her childhood, where have those memories been physically stored? If the neural substrate we thought was necessary for memory is degraded, but the memories can still be accessed, then either our understanding of memory storage is fundamentally wrong, or there’s some resilient substrate we haven’t identified yet.

Right now, around 60 million people have dementia worldwide, and their care costs more than $1 trillion each year. The newest treatments attempt to remove accumulations of abnormally folded proteins in the brain, known as amyloids, which are believed to contribute to Alzheimer’s. One such treatment is lecanemab (brand name Leqembi), which costs around $30,000 per year, in exchange for, at best, a minuscule reduction in the rate of disease progression (let alone actually reversing the decline).

If terminal lucidity is real, it means that there are naturally occurring conditions under which even severely damaged brains can have their function restored. And if a dying brain can indeed spontaneously access ‘lost’ memories, perhaps we could induce a living brain to do the same.

However, there are good reasons to think terminal lucidity might not be real. Primary among these is observer bias.

Watching a parent slowly lose themselves without ever having a final chance to say goodbye is devastating. People crave the deathbed scenes from books and movies: the elderly relative who pronounces meaningful final words to gathered family before peacefully expiring. But there’s often a long gap between when someone loses the ability to communicate and when they die – days, weeks, months or even years in cases of severe dementia. During this time, family members may rehearse what they wish they could say and dream of what they wish they could hear back, desperately hoping for one last sign, however small, that their loved one recognises them or is trying to communicate.

This creates exactly the conditions for observer bias to flourish.

Consider the case of a 12-year-old girl with cancer, reported in a 2024 study of terminal lucidity among children with severe illnesses. The study, from The Journal of Nervous and Mental Disease, was made by the paediatric haematologist-oncologist Philip Roehrs in the US and a team of researchers from around the world. They reported that the girl had been unresponsive for months and was eventually declared dead. However, according to her mother, just before the girl died, she had opened her eyes, mouthed ‘I love you’ and ‘I’m ready to go home,’ and blinked her eyes to answer yes/no questions. The researchers added that the mother ‘appeared to consider these moments as signs of life, despite her daughter’s medical condition.’

Reports of terminal lucidity come from emotionally invested family members or caregivers

No one wants to ask a grieving mother about how confident she truly is that her unresponsive daughter briefly regained awareness before dying. But from a scientific perspective: were the words she mouthed meaningful speech or just involuntary muscle movements? The same kind of question applies to a grandmother who seems to smile and nod (postural reflex?) or a dying spouse who squeezes a hand when told ‘I love you’ (muscle spasm?).

This is the problem with nearly all reports of terminal lucidity: they come from emotionally invested family members or caregivers with strong motivations to perceive communication where there might be none. Those witnessing changes in their loved ones often have no scientific training to distinguish meaningful behaviour from reflexes, and no blinding to prevent bias.

In 2024, Joan M Griffin and other researchers surveyed family caregivers who reported witnessing lucid episodes in dementia patients. They found 51 per cent of these episodes involved communication that ‘made complete sense’, with another 32 per cent making ‘some sense’. Though, keep in mind that 48 per cent of episodes occurred at least six months before death, with only 18 per cent happening in the final week. That means that most of these weren’t ‘terminal’ lucid episodes at all – they’re potentially just part of the normal cognitive fluctuations that occur as dementia progresses.

The scientific evidence we currently have for terminal lucidity leaves us almost entirely with anecdotal reports from biased observers, collected retrospectively. These have not been objectively verified and mostly describe ambiguous behaviours that could arguably be explained by wishful interpretation.

So, how can we explain this phenomenon that has been consistently reported across centuries and cultures? Anecdotal reports of patients who haven’t spoken in years suddenly engaging in complex conversation are hard to dismiss as mere muscle spasms or observer bias. Something appears to be going on beyond pure confabulation.

No one has yet published any neuroscientific recording of terminal lucidity as it happens, so we still have no record of what the brain is doing during an episode. Although any explanation is necessarily speculative, we can make educated guesses based on known and related phenomena.

One explanation relates to brain-swelling reduction. Dying patients often develop brain swelling for multiple reasons, such as electrolyte imbalances, low blood protein, kidney or liver failure, inflammation, or damage to the blood-brain barrier. This swelling compresses brain tissue and reduces blood flow, starving neurons of oxygen and glucose. The result is the familiar progression of terminal delirium: confusion, then sleepiness, then coma, then death.

But in their final days, many patients stop eating and drinking entirely. The resulting dehydration could reduce brain swelling, allowing blood flow to increase, which could temporarily restore some cognitive function – a brief window of lucidity before the dying process continues. It’s a simple mechanism: lower intracranial pressure means better movement of blood through the brain, which means more oxygen and glucose in the brain, which in turn means more functional neurons.

Maybe damaged neural networks can spontaneously reorganise in ways that temporarily restore function

Another explanation, perhaps working in tandem with brain-swelling reduction, relates to how brain networks respond to extreme conditions.

Normal consciousness requires a precise balance of neurochemicals. What is referred to as ‘wakefulness’ – the daily state when you are conscious and your brain is actively responding to the world – depends on brainstem neurons continuously releasing neuromodulators like acetylcholine, noradrenaline and histamine into the cortex. When this system breaks down in a damaged or dying brain, people typically become progressively less responsive.

But sometimes, perturbing a broken system can temporarily fix it. If you’ve ever fixed a glitchy electronic device by hitting it, you’ve seen how pushing a malfunctioning system into an unusual state can accidentally restore function.

Maybe something similar happens in dying brains, where under extreme or unusual conditions, damaged neural networks can spontaneously reorganise in ways that temporarily restore function. One research paper speculates that dying brains might generate ‘spontaneous network integration manifesting as lucid behaviour’ through ‘rapid and nonlinear synchronisation’. Translated from Academic into English, this means something like: ‘Weird things might happen in a dying brain that briefly improve function, but we don’t really know what those things are.’

Even after reading many of the studies about terminal lucidity, I genuinely don’t know whether it really exists. Given this, the appropriate response is neither to credulously accept every report nor to entirely dismiss the phenomenon either. Instead, we need to begin studying terminal lucidity properly. For a long time, almost no one was, though that’s beginning to change.

In 2019, the US National Institute on Aging funded a wave of research, and results are arriving. The most important so far, by a team from the University of Wisconsin-Madison, has captured potential lucid episodes on video. Across 1,433 hours of footage from 20 hospice patients, the team identified nine lucid episodes in three participants – events where communication and social engagement spiked far above each patient’s measured baseline. One man, after a two-week decline, spoke in full sentences for two days, named his family members, said ‘I’m leaving soon,’ and died days later.

This isn’t definitive proof that terminal lucidity is real – the study still suffered from potential observer bias. But it’s the best evidence so far that something is happening that can’t be waved away as grief-soaked confabulation.

What we still don’t have is any evidence of physiological changes during terminal lucidity. There have been no brain scans during an episode, nor blood work to accompany them. A group of researchers at New York University Langone Health, led by Sam Parnia, has been planning continuous EEG monitoring of 500 dying dementia patients, which might someday tell us what brain activity looks like during lucid episodes.

If the video evidence holds up, and if some future study finds a physiological signature to match that evidence, the picture of dementia we currently have would need rethinking. Memory and identity would need to be understood as more distributed, more redundant, and more recoverable than the standard neurodegenerative story allows. And instead of pouring billions into another hopeless amyloid-clearing drug, we might finally have a treatment path worth pursuing – if only we can discover how to stretch a lucid episode into a lasting return.

item.title: Say yes to regret
item.dc:creator: Sandra Lamb
item.description:
After my husband died, I fell into a dark ruminative spiral. The way back would begin at 2pm tomorrow

- by Sandra Lamb

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
The phone rang five times, and then it rang some more. I was calling from Charlotte, North Carolina – wedged into the cracked-leather passenger seat of a friend’s Honda, my suitcase still exhaling the recycled-air odour of the airport – trying to reach Charles at home in Denver. It was eight in the morning in Denver, long past the time he’d normally be stirring raisins into his oatmeal, waiting for his toast to brown.

Six rings. Seven. Eight. Each one twisted something in my chest.

We’d had words that morning as he drove me to the airport – one of those marital skirmishes that feels urgent and forgettable at the same time, but leaves a residue.

On the 10th ring, there was a clatter – the sound of the receiver being knocked, fumbled, dragged across the nightstand. Then Charles’s voice, dry as autumn leaves: ‘Hello.’

Even through the phone line, I could hear the sleep thick in his throat. I apologised for waking him.

‘I need to cancel my appointment this morning,’ he rasped.

‘Don’t worry,’ I countered. ‘I’ll call. Just go back to sleep.’

I told him I loved him, hoping he heard an apology tucked inside those three syllables – a white flag folded and slipped between the words – for my role in the dustup. He said something I couldn’t quite make out. Then the line went dead.

Charles was having three kinds of days then: good days, not-so-good days, and what he called ‘soldiering on’ days. I couldn’t tell which this was, but he was fine when I left, and we’d agreed I should make this trip. We’d bought tickets to California for the following weekend – relatives in Lodi expecting us. He’d also rented and paid a full month’s fee for a condo in Palm Springs for the following month.

But nothing was normal. Charles was undergoing chemotherapy for cancer, and though he seemed to be tolerating the treatments most of the time, his determination to get well had a quality I recognised: the same straightness of spine and iron resolve he’d maintained through one family crisis after another.

Seven years earlier, we’d sat in a small examining room painted institutional green. With clinical precision, Han Myint, the oncologist, delivered the diagnosis of mantle cell non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma: ‘You have two choices. Do nothing, and you’ll live less than a year. Or do a stem cell transplant, and you’ll have two, maybe three years.’

I sobbed so violently the chair legs stuttered against the tile floor

Charles didn’t blink. He sat straight-backed on the examining table, absorbing this news the way he’d absorbed everything else: his first son Mark’s paranoid schizophrenia and subsequent suicide attempts over a decade; the day Mark bought lighter fluid, walked to City Park, doused himself, and struck a match. Then came the second son, Douglas – another diagnosis of paranoid schizophrenia, another series of treatment failures.

I had no such resolve. I bent double in my chair and sobbed so violently the chair legs stuttered against the tile floor.

What followed was an exhaustive campaign. We interviewed doctors, toured cancer centres, compared treatment protocols with the forensic attentiveness of detectives. We settled on Anschutz Hospital at the University of Colorado Medical Center, and Charles began the regimen: three rounds of chemo, then a month hospitalised for the stem cell transplant.

For a while, it seemed to be working. Then his platelet count plummeted. His balance tilted. His memory became unreliable.

Still, we didn’t talk about death. We talked about the next infusion, the chest port installation, the small-print protocols of infection prevention: no movie theatres; no handshaking; wearing a mask everywhere. We were living in the present tense – the grammatical tense of hope deferred: if we could just get through this treatment, when his platelet count improves, after he recovers.

All that day in Charlotte, I tried calling him again. With each ring, the knot in my stomach squeezed and roiled, until the phone kicked to my own recorded voice: ‘Sorry, no one is available at the moment…’ By late afternoon, alarm was coiling through my chest like smoke. I called the neighbours. ‘Would you please use the garage code and enter the garage?’ I started, after Dean answered, trying to keep panic from seeping into the edges of my voice. ‘If Charles’s car is gone, everything’s fine. But if it’s there, would you please go inside and check on him?’

The next five minutes felt like 50. When my cell phone rang, Dean’s voice had that careful flatness people use when delivering catastrophic news: ‘He’s here. In bed. Unconscious. We’ve called 911.’

We stayed on the line until the EMTs arrived. One of them, Brad, took the phone and began rapid-firing questions. Then: ‘He’s unresponsive. We’re taking him to the hospital.’ ‘Anschutz Hospital,’ I inserted. ‘The 11th-floor cancer ward. They’re expecting him.’ At Brad’s hesitation, I added: ‘Those are his doctor’s instructions.’

There were muffled voices, an exchange I couldn’t hear, then Brad was back. The weather in Denver was bad, he said. Roads were impassable. ‘We’re only authorised to take him to the local hospital,’ he concluded. Swedish Hospital was four miles away. Anschutz was 10.

The first United flight out of Charlotte the next morning got me to Denver by 10 am, and I drove straight to Swedish, still in yesterday’s clothes; still carrying the low-grade static charge of panic.

Charles lay in the critical care unit, his skin the chalky-white colour of copy paper, connected to an octopus of machinery – tubes and monitors that rhythmically wheezed and beeped. I looked anxiously for something in his handsome face that would give us possibility.

When I asked to talk to his doctor, a nurse slid her eyes away from mine and told me he had a ‘care team’ that made rounds ‘very early’ each morning. No specific doctor. No one I could meet with, she added. When I asked about transferring Charles, she replied only that his medical records from Anschutz had been requested.

His first words were: ‘I want to go home.’ Instead, he was transferred to a rehab

On day four, I learned that the computerised record systems of Swedish and Anschutz weren’t compatible.

On day five, Charles regained consciousness. His first words were: ‘I want to go home.’ Instead, he was transferred to a rehab. There he contracted MRSA. Standing beside his bed, holding his hand, I watched the monitor numbers falter and drop – 92, 89, 85 – as his chest heaved for breath. He went into shock. They ordered me out of the room, gave him a tracheostomy, rushed him to critical care. He died several hours later.

The regrets started immediately, a relentless, punishing drumbeat: I should not have gone to Charlotte. Why didn’t I scream into the phone demanding the EMTs take him to Anschutz. I should have had his records immediately couriered to Swedish. I should have insisted on transferring him to Anschutz the moment I arrived at Swedish. I should have assembled a home care team, checked him out of the hospital, and taken him home. I should have said ‘I’m sorry’ for my role in our airport-ride dispute.

It was too late. I was guilty. I was a very bad person.

What I was experiencing has a clinical name I later learned – one that researchers have spent decades untangling from grief itself. Rumination: the mental habit of repetitively focusing on the causes and consequences of distress without moving toward resolution.

The immediate mountain of death logistics required laser focus – the funeral home, the casket, the flowers, the military honours, the graveside burial. After the taps at the graveside service, I placed a single red rose on the coffin; came home to an empty house. Making it as far as the den sofa, I collapsed, unable to will myself to do even the simplest thing or stop the parade of negative regrets.

Nights were the worst. I’d stagger to bed well after midnight, then wake at 2.30 am to accusations that marched through my mind until dawn. During the day, I didn’t answer the phone. Didn’t keep appointments. Didn’t finish notifying people. Didn’t file death certificates.

After three months, in desperation, I signed up for a grief class at church. Eight of us sat in a circle of folding chairs while a facilitator asked us to name what we had lost. I couldn’t stop at one thing. The class didn’t slow the spiral – it deepened it. I had moved past ordinary grief into something denser and more airless: a self-reinforcing, ruminative loop. Misery, it turns out, is a learnable skill.

Regret can be a compass if you let it point you toward a specific plan of action

One night I stood in the shaft of the medicine cabinet’s overhead light and counted out Charles’s leftover pain pills. Thirty. I held them in my hand. What brought me back was Charles – his unambiguous sense of right and wrong. He had fought for a refund clause in the Palm Springs rental contract, insisting on it with the same care he brought to everything he wanted to protect. Honouring that felt like honouring him. This was something I could do. Must do. Here, at last, was a possible path back. I returned the pills to the bottle, walked to my desk, and wrote in my Day-Timer: ‘Call owner at 2 pm tomorrow.’

Then I slept.

The next day at 2 pm, the owner didn’t answer my call. Then he ignored my follow-up emails and phone calls. When I did finally get him on the phone, he suggested brightly that perhaps I’d like to come stay by myself now. It would be a good change for me, he said. He would change the lease dates. He was not going to refund our money as he’d promised Charles, that was crystal clear. I filed a complaint, showed up, pushed back. Each concrete step felt like a cable pulling me, hand over hand, out of rumination.

Do I still have regrets? Yes – mostly about the things I didn’t do, the tender words I left unsaid, the presence I failed to offer. The missteps are easier to carry now. But I learned something durable: regret is not a verdict. It can be a compass if you let it point you toward a specific plan of action. Asking ‘why’ questions – the endless, recursive circling through the same worn grooves – is rumination, and it deepens its own channel the more you travel it.

But the questions that matter are different: What can I do? What, specifically, will I do tomorrow at 2 pm? These interrupt the pattern. The next time regret comes – and it will, as reliably and certainly as a change in the weather – I know how to say yes to it, to find my way back.

item.title: My name is Annabel
item.dc:creator: Psyche Video
item.description:
A creative collaboration between participant and filmmaker explores how it feels to live and perform with Down syndrome

- Directed by Ida Joglar

Watch on Psyche
item.content:encoded: When asked what kind of film she would make, Annabel Hernandez had a simple answer: one with her family, her friends and music, of course. In My Name is Annabel, the filmmaker Ida Joglar helps Hernandez, who has Down syndrome, bring her artistic vision to life. Joglar follows Hernandez around her home city of Wichita, Kansas as she auditions for a play, works at her grandparents’ ice cream shop and spends time at a day programme for adults with intellectual disabilities. Hernandez also sits down for a series of conversations with her friends and family, which touch on everything from their favourite TV shows to bigger questions about what it means to live with, or love someone with, Down syndrome. And, ever the passionate performer, Hernandez even closes things out with her very own music video.

item.title: How to uncover your blind spots
item.dc:creator: Jennifer Farrell
item.description:
We all have parts of ourselves others know but we don’t. Gain greater self-awareness by seeing yourself from the outside in

- by Jennifer Farrell

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
Have you ever been caught off guard by what someone observed about you? Perhaps they described a version of you, or a particular aspect, that didn’t align with your view of yourself. Moments like these can result in a range of feelings, from anxiety and frustration to surprise and curiosity. Often, this other person has pointed out a figurative ‘blind spot’: something about you that you haven’t been able to see clearly.

A friend might casually refer to you as ‘the quiet one’ in the group, even though you’ve never thought of yourself that way. A romantic partner might note, unexpectedly, that you’re quick to agree to what others want. Or a colleague could reveal that people at work find you intimidating. Examples such as these represent blind spots to the extent that they are both surprising to hear and reflect something true about you.

I’ve seen this kind of reveal happen in real time, in a therapy group for students that I run at our college counselling centre. In one session, Nathan* presented in his typical, assured manner, offering support to other group members as they talked about the challenges they were going through. I noticed another member watching him intently and invited her to disclose her thoughts. She expressed feeling ‘useless’ to Nathan. ‘He seems to have it all together,’ she said. ‘We can’t offer him any help.’ Other members nodded in agreement. Nathan seemed surprised, but engaged. He was starting to recognise something about his willingness to be vulnerable – something he had not seen himself.

Self-knowledge comes, in part, from others

One classic model for thinking about self-awareness and how it relates to others is the Johari Window. Introduced in 1955 by the psychologists Joseph Luft and Harrington Ingham (whose first names, combined, form ‘Johari’), the model describes four quadrants, like four sections of a window. These are:

  • an ‘open’ area that includes the aspects of yourself known to you and others;
  • a ‘hidden’ area that includes parts known only to you;
  • an ‘unknown’ area outside of your and everyone else’s awareness; and
  • a ‘blind spot’ – the parts of yourself that you don’t see, but others do.

Everyone has blind spots. After all, we see ourselves and our intentions from the inside out, others experience us from the outside in, and those views cannot be perfectly in sync. Of course, not everyone will perceive you the same way, or with the same clarity, so blind spots are also somewhat subjective. We have to be careful in deciding whose views to take seriously.

As a psychologist, I’ve witnessed the long-term value of facing and understanding the unfamiliar aspects of ourselves. Sometimes, learning about a blind spot is relatively pleasant, even if it’s challenging to wrap your mind around. If you struggle to view yourself positively, you might not see how competent or kind you really are until someone brings it to your attention. In other cases, learning about a blind spot is uncomfortable, and might provoke a defensive response (That can’t be true, I’m not like that…) One of my roles as a therapist is to help clients understand how they might be affecting and coming across to others without their awareness. This can be disarming. As one client put it: ‘It’s like someone just told me I’ve been walking around with food on my face for years and I had no idea.’ Yet learning what others notice about us gives us the opportunity to consider whether our behaviours are truly aligned with what we intend – and where, or whether, we want to adjust.

Pursuing greater self-awareness can feel both risky and exciting. In this Guide, I’ll share some strategies you can use, questions you can ask yourself and others, and important things to remember as you seek wise insights.

item.title: Why women’s laughter has long been treated as a threat
item.dc:creator: Abílio Almeida
item.description:
Traditional patriarchy has always told women not to laugh. Today, female laughter still disturbs a male-dominated world

- by Abílio Almeida

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
My grandmother, Tina, was born in the 1930s in a small village in northern Portugal. She had a difficult life. Widowed young, she was forced to raise 13 children on her own. She wore black until almost the end of her life. In my childhood memories, her face had only two expressions: ‘sad’ and ‘stern’. The first was constant; the second appeared whenever she scolded us.

I grew up without ever seeing her laugh. As a child, I assumed this was natural. Silence and emotional restraint seemed woven into her character. Only later did I begin to understand that this was not merely a trait of my grandmother’s, but the result of wider beliefs and social expectations that, for generations, deprived many women of the freedom to express something that had belonged to them since birth: their laughter.

I have often returned to those childhood memories of her lack of laughter. They stayed with me so deeply that, years later, they became the starting point for my PhD research into how laughter is shaped by culture and media.

When I was living and studying in London, I remember having many conversations with friends (and friends of friends) about their own memories of non-laughing grandmothers. I found echoes of my own story in accounts from Saudi Arabia, Japan and many other countries around the world: stories of grandmothers who were permanently serious, or of other women whose laughter was absent, inappropriate or out of place.

Of the many accounts I have gathered, one stands out. A Spanish friend told me that her grandmother began to laugh only after developing dementia. ‘I preferred that version of her,’ she confessed. ‘She stopped being rigid; she began to laugh and became more light-hearted.’

We may think of laughter as one of the simplest human impulses – spontaneous, joyful, harmless. So how did women’s laughter, especially in Europe, come to be treated with such deep suspicion?

Over the years, I have heard many explanations. Some have argued that prohibitions on laughter were a Latin or Catholic inheritance – and one that did not affect only women. There is some truth in that. For a long time, social norms spread by the Church suggested that positive emotional responses, like laughter, expressed a temporary enjoyment of worldly things and, therefore, a visible threat to moral purity. In the eyes of the medieval Church, as Umberto Eco suggests in his novel The Name of the Rose (1980), laughter could be seen as a kind of daytime orgasm or ejaculation, the waking counterpart to the nocturnal emissions (ie, wet dreams) that doctrine excused as involuntary, and a shameful public display of earthly pleasure, uncontrolled by spiritual discipline.

But that reading is reductive. Women’s emotional expressions in general, and their laughter in particular, have often been policed more closely than men’s.

To understand this history, it is worth looking at some of the pillars that shaped the Western feminine emotional ideal. Athenagoras of Athens, who lived around 115 to 190 CE, argued that a man should approach a woman in the same way a farmer approaches the land: not for pleasure, but only to sow his seed. In his view, woman was merely ‘ground’ – something that does not desire, does not feel, does not choose, and exists only to reproduce. We are speaking here of the feminine ideal in intimate life, but the same ideas applied socially. At one point, the Archbishop of Constantinople John Chrysostom, who lived around 347 to 407 CE, observed that women barely dared to laugh in the presence of their husbands. He even expressed discomfort at seeing them do so during his sermons. It is therefore unsurprising that later manuals, such as Le Ménagier de Paris (c1393) and The Ladies’ Book of Etiquette, and Manual of Politeness (1860), promoted a feminine ideal in which laughing freely and openly could not, ultimately, exist within society.

Stories about the risks deprived women of laughter not only in public, but also in their own homes

When we look at the Western tradition of writers and thinkers – especially those who were influenced by Plato – we frequently find laughter associated with a loss of control and distance from reason and sacred things. In a world organised through hierarchies, where man owed reverence to God and woman to man, female laughter was seen as a threat to that order. The fact that women’s laughter continues to be more heavily scrutinised today suggests that traces of this medieval vision still remain.

Maggie Hennefeld, professor of cultural studies and comparative literature at the University of Minnesota, notes that between the mid-19th and early 20th centuries, accounts circulated claiming that hundreds of women had died from laughter. She writes:

For example, in 1893, Bertha Pruett was entertaining guests at her home in Philadelphia, one of whom, a young man, was ‘a noted wit. One of his remarks threw Miss Pruett into a violent fit of laughter, which lasted some minutes, when it suddenly changed to a cry of pain, and she fell to the floor. Blood gushed from her nose and mouth and medical assistance was summoned, but before anything could be done … she was dead’ … Stories such as these, evidently, revealed women’s laughter to be fatal.

It is easy to imagine the impact of such painful stories. Undoubtedly, such stories about the risks of laughter deprived women of laughter not only in public, but also in their own homes. Many must have lived in fear of laughing, since – according to those narratives – the consequences could be fatal. Some women, according to certain accounts, died simply for laughing at jokes about mothers-in-law.

In the study ‘Gender and the Evaluation of Humor at Work’ (2019), Jonathan B Evans and colleagues found that, in the workplace, making others laugh tends to increase men’s status while diminishing that of women. As for laughter itself, something similar occurs in public life. In contemporary political contexts, figures such as Hillary Clinton and Kamala Harris have been repeatedly scrutinised for their laughter, in a way that is rarely applied to their male counterparts. Few people today would openly tell women not to laugh or make others laugh. Yet both actions still seem to disturb a masculinised atmosphere whose pressure may not always be immediately obvious but is still felt in certain places and by certain people.

Why might this happen? In Laughter (1900), Henri Bergson suggests that laughter marks the breaking of social rigidity and exposes the artificiality of social norms. We might therefore understand laughter as the sound of that rigidity giving way, like glass breaking. The person who laughs at the way things are is able to momentarily step outside the established order and, from that position, reveal how constructed it really is: a peasant laughing at a king, a worker laughing at a boss, a woman laughing at a world that expects her to be silent. In such moments, human nature asserts itself over social constructions, and whatever hierarchies were in place are briefly suspended. Perhaps that is why, throughout history, laughter in general, and women’s laughter in particular, has unsettled so many people. Laughter is, after all, the sound of social rigidity cracking under the pressure of human nature.

Though laughter has historically been seen as dangerous and unsettling, it has firmly established itself in the modern world. This change has been generated, in part, by the rise of new forms of media.

In the early 20th century, cinema emerged as a powerful tool for weakening older fears around laughter and unleashing its liberating force. Women attending movies during that period could see, with their own eyes, people like them laughing on screen. They watched them laugh without any negative consequence befalling them and, more importantly, without succumbing to a laughter-induced death. In this way, the laughter present in cinema was important for many women who, symbolically at least, did not yet know what laughter really was. And comedy films brought a new and uplifting message of hope, power and prominence to laughter, the opposite of what had often been heard until then. This was true for both women and men, but especially for women, whose laughter had been more restricted. The arrival of comedies on television only accelerated this process.

Morning talk shows filled with small acts of silliness played a crucial role in my grandmother’s transformation

Think of the laughter running through the US TV comedy I Love Lucy in the 1950s, the Mexican comedy El Chavo del Ocho in the 1970s, or the British comedy Keeping Up Appearances in the 1990s. Think also of the many daytime talk shows that proliferated across television screens around the world in the late 20th century, where laughter and tears are as common as words. What elite culture has often dismissed as frivolous media content – easy laughter, excessive emotionality – has played an important role in the democratisation of emotions in general, and laughter in particular, in the past century. For millions of people, the arrival of cinema, radio, television and, more recently, social media has served as a source of emotional literacy in both personal and social life.

As for my grandmother, her beliefs deprived her for practically her entire life not only of comfortable access to the social world but, above all, of a genuine connection to her own emotional world. Only later in life did she truly begin to laugh. What helped was her favourite television programmes – morning talk shows filled with recipes, domestic advice, laughter and small acts of silliness – which played a crucial role in that transformation. Through the easy laughter she consumed, she slowly learned to laugh without fear or embarrassment.

That daily exposure helped free her from the constraints of a certain cultural and religious pressure she never knew how to name, but which had kept her enclosed within herself, distant from her own body and her own nature.

I cannot say exactly when I first saw her laugh openly. But I remember her last laugh. It was in hospital, when I asked whether the hotel service was good enough for her requirements. It was not a good joke, I know, but it was enough to make her laugh. And laugh she did – without embarrassment, without covering her face, without fear of dying.

item.description:
How Father Michael Shanahan reconciled his identity with the Catholic Church’s position on homosexuality

- Directed by John Haley

Watch on Psyche
item.content:encoded: For Father Michael Shanahan, coming out as gay occurred slowly, over decades. The process began with recognising a tension in himself, continued with confiding in his immediate family, and culminated in openly identifying as a gay Catholic priest. In The Longest Walk, Shanahan shares this story, including how, in the depths of prayer, he handled the conflict between his calling to the priesthood and the Catholic Church’s official position that homosexual attraction is an ‘objective disorder’ – a crisis that required its own leap of faith to resolve. Combining archival imagery from Shanahan’s life and contemporary footage of him conducting mass in Chicago, the US director John Haley forms a spare yet complex meditation on identity and belief.

item.title: Impatience is an emotion, not a trait
item.dc:creator: Amy Arthur
item.description:
Watching Penelope’s heroic wait in The Odyssey made me lament my impatience. But maybe I’ve been thinking about it wrong

- by Amy Arthur

Read on Psyche
item.content:encoded:
Last month, while watching Christopher Nolan’s new epic The Odyssey, I couldn’t help but marvel at the patience of Penelope, who waits 20 years for her husband – the king, Odysseus – to return to Ithaca. Despite no indication of when, or if, he might return, she is steadfast in her wait.

I cannot claim such patience. My husband has never left me to manage a kingdom, but I’ve been plagued by plenty of frustrating waits. I am as impatient about small delays, like queueing at the post office, as I am about the longer, life-altering ones. I remember how exasperated I felt by the multiple delays in moving to our first home, not to mention my impatience now at waiting nine years for an endometriosis diagnosis.

I’ve long assumed that impatience is simply part of my personality. But I recently came across a different perspective: according to the psychologist Kate Sweeny and her colleagues at the University of California, Riverside, impatience is not a fixed facet of who we are. Instead, it’s an emotion – and patience is the process by which we manage it. While this isn’t a novel theory, Sweeny’s team tested it recently with promising results – they found, for instance, that it’s not so much the length of the wait that matters, but how fair we consider it to be.

I find the implications hopeful. Just as we can learn to handle other unpleasant emotions, we can all develop better skills and techniques to deal with impatience.

As with other difficult emotions, one key to regulating impatience is likely to be acknowledging it in the first place. We see this in Penelope: she allows herself to feel the impatience, but finds a way through it. The next time I’m faced with a long delay, I’ll channel my inner Greek queen and know that it’s an emotion I can manage, even if I can’t control the wait itself.
